b0deea04c96bb290: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.
Transparency, monetized

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.

The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.
The AI detection problem

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”
Everything’s on the table

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”
a9e97e808dea3e7c: A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.
The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its plans for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.
One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video.

This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis.

As any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not currently needed for on-demand streaming platforms.

The government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference.

TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction.

Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal.

"The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," said NUJ general secretary Laura Davison.

Many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere says more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading. Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says.

Another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of.

"Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," said Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury.

"Alternatively, in the context of ongoing cost of living pressures in the UK, the government could opt to reduce the price of the fee payable by the extended pool of consumers. Coupled with a reformed enforcement mechanism that effectively reduces evasion, this would still improve the BBC's financial outlook relative to the status quo."
Earlier this year, the government revealed that it was planning for a switch-off of the broadcast digital terrestrial television (DTT) service in the future.

This is again because of the rapidly changing nature of the TV landscape, with viewers shifting to online streaming, creating a hybrid landscape between IPTV, traditional DTT, satellite broadcasting, and cable.
Current licenses for DTT services expire at the end of December, 2034, but the government may choose to extend them to 2044. ®
afccdcb010158c67: If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home
Originally published on Global Voices
Court of Appeal building in Lagos, Nigeria. Image by King ChristLike via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This post by Fatima Zahra Yahaya is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In February 2025, a letter from a jailed man named Thomas Jonathan Biodun reached the public after some Nigerian Twitter influencers visited his prison to play a friendly football match with the inmates. Biodun was in jail over a debt of NGN 1,137,000 (USD 758). In the letter, he said he had asked for help online before, but someone had called him a scammer.

One of the influencers shared the letter on social media. Another influencer, Sir Dickson, who goes by the handle Wizarab10 on X, pushed it further, garnering over 2.5 million views in one post. In his post, Sir Dickson said, “Nobody should be in prison over a debt. It is not a criminal offense. I have spoken to @egi_nupe [another X influencer and lawyer], and we will be taking it up. Imagine rotting in prison because you’re poor.” A public donation campaign followed, and within weeks, it had raised enough money to clear the debt.
Punch Newspapers reported that Biodun walked out of Apapa Kirikiri Correctional Center and thanked everyone who helped.
Biodun’s story has a happy ending. But it raises a hard question: Should a person’s freedom depend on the benevolence of internet strangers and how many people share a post?
The problem behind this story

In February 2026, the Nigerian Correctional Service said that most people in its custody were still waiting for trial. Many of them have not been found guilty of any crime but remain in pre-trial detention. While some of them cannot pay bail, others cannot pay court fines. In Nigeria, the crime of being poor can land you in a jail cell.

Waiting is not a small thing. While a case drags on, a person may lose their job, business, or place to live. A family can lose its breadwinner, which can derail a whole family — or even a whole community’s livelihoods.
When the internet steps in
Jonathan Biodun is not the only person who turned to the internet to seek support for injustice.

Quadri Alabi, 17, went viral in 2023 when he stood in front of former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi’s campaign convoy. He spent months in Kirikiri Prison over a robbery charge that his lawyer, Inibehe Effiong, called baseless. Effiong also said the police recorded him under the wrong age, meaning he was charged and sentenced as an adult. On April 17, 2025, he was freed. The same day, Effiong asked the public on X to help his family move to a safer home, because they were still getting threats. The International Center for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) reported that more than NGN 3 million (over USD 21,965) was raised within two hours.

Emeka Nzeruike was arrested in 2015, when he was only 12 years old, over an alleged theft. He spent 10 years in prison waiting for trial. In July 2025, a lawyer named Alexander Nzeadi, who posts on X as @_youfoundalex, took up his case, and Emeka walked out of court.

The lawyer wrote that Emeka had been alone, afraid, and forgotten, with no trial and no lawyer. He then asked Nigerians to help Emeka heal, learn a skill, and start his life again now that he was finally free. The post was seen millions of times.
The other side of the story

Look closely at these cases. Biodun, Alabi, and Nzeruike were helped because their stories reached the right people. A letter found the right hands. A lawyer or a kind stranger posted at the right time.
Biodun said he was first called a scammer. That shows how difficult it can be to be believed online.
But what about the person nobody posts about? Not every inmate has a famous friend, a lawyer, or a loud voice to advocate on their behalf. For them, it can feel like no one is watching.
This is the worry. If help comes only to the stories that go viral, then luck decides who goes home. A sad story with a clear photo may win hearts, while a quiet case may be missed.
Raising money to pay for inmates’ legal fees or fines is not new, and it is not only done online.

In 2023, The Conclave reported that public-spirited people and a group called Prisoners Rehabilitation and Welfare Action (PRAWA), a non-governmental organization (NGO), paid fines to free 37 inmates from Kuje and Suleja prisons. The Interior Minister at the time had urged Nigerians to pay the fines of some prisoners to ease crowding in prisons.
Kindness is good. But justice should not depend on luck or others’ generosity.
A hope for smart leaders

I do not believe we should stop being kind. I believe we should fix the courts, so that kindness is not the only hope a poor person has. If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home.
Social media is already doing one useful thing. It shows us real faces and real stories where the system is failing. Smart leaders, lawyers, and judges can listen, and they can fix it.
Until then, every shared post is a sign that Nigerians care. It is also a sign that the courts must do better. Everyone in Nigeria deserves a fair day in court.
Written by Guest Contributor
ca171ab41a233d37: LONDON, Nov 25 — Household energy bills for millions of Britons are set to surge by more than a quarter from January, the sector regulator Ofgem announced today, as the Middle East war drives up wholesale gas prices.
The US-Iran conflict, which sharply reduced tanker traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz, has sent oil and gas prices soaring and raised concerns about a fresh spike in overall inflation.
Ofgem, which sets every quarter the price cap that suppliers can charge customers for electricity and gas, said the cap would increase 26 per cent in January.
That will add around £443 (RM2,385) to the typical annual bill, which will climb to about £2,166, Ofgem said.

“Conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher, and we know this price increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches,” said Ofgem’s director general for markets, Neil Kenward.

The increase will impact around 20 million households on standard contracts with variable tariffs. A further 10 million households on fixed-rate deals will be shielded from the rise as long as their contract remains in place.
The price hike means that millions of households will face higher payments even after the government hands out direct subsidies of £100 towards energy bills.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government announced the one-off payment for 20 million households in its annual budget report in October, while also removing fixed fees on gas bills.
The government has also extended a temporary tax cut on household electricity prices.

Since the outbreak of the US-Iran war on 28 February, the price of European natural gas, measured by the Dutch TTF futures contract, has surged by around 190 per cent, rising to €92 per megawatt-hour from around €32.
Britain’s annual inflation rate reached a 12-month high in October at 3.6 per cent as the Middle East conflict drove up motor fuel costs.
The latest energy price cap increase is set to fuel inflation further next year, adding to cost-of-living pressures.
However, gas prices remain well below the levels seen at the height of the energy crisis in 2022 after Russia began its invasion of Ukraine.
The sharpest increase in the price cap came in October 2022, when it was raised by 80 per cent. — AFP

7f46162ddd2d3fe1: A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

This case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of New York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision says Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors showed evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”

Another item of evidence apparently showed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”
Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

Huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ says.

The feds say the Chinese company also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”
Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.”
“The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds.
Sentencing will take place in September 2027.

The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA.

Washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese company return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®

c33bcd47cf0102df: VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues.
VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks:
Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.

The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs.
This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off.
Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

3e6bca11ce95d356: Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the company’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

In chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew.

The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.
Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.”

Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO said the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”

News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix announced its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®
2c678e870b907039: Soal KLSCAH yang sengaja dijadikan isu masih bising. Oleh kerana kebisingan, saya rasa kenalah tulis sikit hal ini. Kuala Lumpur & Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall atau Dewan Perhimpunan Cina Kuala Lumpur dan Selangor berasal dari nama Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall, ditukar kepada nama sekarang pada 2006.

Secara ringkas, ia merupakan pertubuhan bukan berasaskan keuntungan, dan pusat komuniti yang penting bagi masyarakat Cina di Kuala Lumpur dan Selangor. Selain menaungi puluhan atau mungkin juga ratusan persatuan Cina tempatan, KLSCAH aktif menganjurkan acara kebudayaan, forum serta dialog. Selain dialog berkenaan hubungan antara kaum dan hak asasi manusia, ia juga menyentuh beberapa isu nasional yang tidak disenangi pemerintah khususnya kerajaan Barisan Nasional dulu.
Pentas KLSCAH pernah digunakan dalam menuntut Akta Keselamatan Dalam Negeri dimansuhkan. Semasa Dr Mahathir Mohamad menentang Najib Razak bersabit skandal 1MDB, beliau bercakap di atas pentas KLSCAH.

Pemuda Umno memang ada 'sejarah tidak manis' dengan KLSCAH. Contoh: Pada 2001, Pemuda Umno mengadakan demonstrasi di hadapan bangunan KLSCAH bagi memprotes terhadap apa yang dikenali sebagai agenda 17 perkara yang diperjuangkan oleh Jawatankuasa Rayuan Pilihan Raya Pertubuhan Pertubuhan Cina Malaysia, yang lebih dikenali sebagai Suqiu.

Pemuda Umno tuduh Suqiu mempersoalkan hak keistimewaan orang Melayu. Suqiu menafikan. Pemuda Umno tetap berdemonstrasi di KLSCAH. Meskipun aman dengan kawalan polis, tetapi kata-kata kesat dan ancaman dilemparkan. Ertinya demonstrasi berbaur perkauman.
Jadi apabila Pemuda Umno zaman sekarang membantah soal premium bagi pembaharuan pajakan tanah KLSCAH, ia bukan sesuatu yang memeranjatkan. Bagi saya it's expected.

Meskipun banyak penjelasan telah diberi pelbagai pihak termasuk kerajaan khususnya Menteri Wilayah Persekutan Hannah Yeoh, Pemuda Umno dan golongan serta kumpulan sewaktu dengannya tidak berpuas hati. Ia dijadikan isu politik bersandar ras. Identity politics is alive and kicking. Sungguh sedih.

Saya tidak bercadang menghuraikan bantahan pihak yang membantah mahupun penjelasan pihak yang menjelaskan. Rasanya ramai yang sudah maklum. Saya cuma mahu mengutarakan pandangan aktivis Seniman Paksi Rakyat, Kassim Muhamad. Paksi ialah pertubuhan seni dan budaya yang diasaskan sasterawan dan penggiat teater, Che Shamsudin Othman atau Dinsman, dan menggerakkan aktiviti sastera, teater, dan kesenian berteraskan isu masyarakat serta budaya tanah air. In short, Seniman Paksi Rakyat is a Malay NGO.

Kata Kassim: "Kami di Paksi kenal KLSCAH semasa kami berjuang membantah isu pembangunan oleh kerajaan Umno di kampung tradisional di Gombak. Kami bersama arwah Cikgu Ishak Surin, isu PPSMI dan juga isu bahasa ibunda."

To put things in context, PPSMI ialah Pengajaran dan Pembelajaran Sains dan Matematik dalam bahasa Inggeris. Paksi antara badan yang menentang keras dasar itu. Walaupun saya tidak setuju dengan bantahan mereka, saya hormat pendirian dan usaha Paksi. PPSMI dimulakan pada 2003 di bawah pentadbiran Mahathir tetapi dimansuhkan pada 2012 untuk digantikan dengan dasar Memartabatkan Bahasa Malaysia Memperkukuhkan Bahasa Inggeris.

'Cikgu Ishak Surin' yang Kassim sebut itu seorang aktivis politik dan sosial yang konsisten menyumbang kepada perjuangan untuk rakyat. Bertanya si Kassim: "Ya tanah KLSCAH ini milik persatuan Cina. Ada masalah?"

Obviously, ada as far as Umno and friends are concerned. Semalam Hannah Yeoh semasa memberi penjelasan di Parlimen berkata isu KLSCAH dijadikan isu panas hanya kerana menterinya (yang mengendali soal ini) berbangsa Cina dan daripada DAP. Saya setuju.

Kata Kassim: "Semasa YB Hannah Yeoh angkat isu Sungai Penchala, puak-puak yang bising sekarang ini sunyi dan sepi. Tentu ada sebabnya kenapa sunyi dan bisu. Sebabnya ia tak boleh jadi modal politik." Tepat sekali kata beliau.

Isu utama berkaitan Sungai Penchala pada 2026 tertumpu kepada kajian pengezonan kampung tradisi oleh Dewan Bandaraya Kuala Lumpur, risiko banjir kilat serta kerja menaik taraf sungai dan masalah pencemaran air.
Keputusan dan hala tuju pembangunan bergantung kepada pandangan serta persetujuan penduduk dan pemilik tanah melalui sesi libat urus. Penduduk dan pemilik tanah ialah orang Melayu.

Sejak menjadi Ahli Parlimen Segambut, Yeoh menyuarakan cadangan mengiktiraf Kampung Sungai Penchala sebagai kampung warisan Melayu dan menggesa kawasan pembangunan selari dengan kapasiti prasarana dan tidak menghakis ciri kampung tradisional.

Isu KLSCAH yang sedang dibisingkan sekarang, selain oleh kerana menteri berketurunan Cina dan partinya DAP, ia juga pada hemat saya dilabel oleh golongan yang buat bising sebagai isu yang 'memanjakan' masyarakat Cina lalu mesti ditentang.
Tentangan hanya untuk mendapat keuntungan politik murahan.

a65f509715b5b41f: Patrick T. Fallon/GettyIt’s hard to think of Nvidia without picturing Jensen Huang. Rarely seen without his signature black leather jacket, Huang has led chipmaker Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, turning it into a central player in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Earlier this month, Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of Nvidia’s board, in the wake of a bombshell scandal involving affairs and alleged corporate espionage. Days later, the board linked his departure to “personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”. It said it did “not intend to reinstate” him. This week, however, it voted unanimously to bring him back, following a remarkable intervention by US President Donald Trump. Many analysts have already weighed in on why the US government intervened. But there’s a deeper, more fundamental question here about corporate power. If a chief executive is seen as too valuable to lose, can a company’s board still hold them to account? If it can’t, what exactly is the board for? Read more: Trump had 4 reasons to ‘convince’ Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang. Here’s why it matters globally The ‘key person risk’ Sometimes, the “hero” leader of a company can become its biggest vulnerability. In corporate governance, this is called “key person risk”. It is the danger a company comes to depend so heavily on one person that losing them would do serious damage. This problem often grows out of success. A founder who builds a business and shapes its culture becomes its public face. Staff, customers and investors start to see the person and the company as one. Think of Steve Jobs, co-founder and longtime chief executive of Apple, or even the fictional media magnate Logan Roy in the TV series Succession. Nvidia itself recognised this risk before Huang’s brief removal. Its 2026 annual report warned the company was “highly dependent on the services” of its longstanding executive team, and that failing “to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions” could hinder its success in the long term. Despite this, when Huang left, no permanent successor was ready. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in temporarily while the board searched for a replacement. Who’s watching the boss? So, what is a board actually for? Shareholders can’t supervise the managers in a large company like Nvidia; instead, they elect a board of directors to do it for them. While the board isn’t involved in daily operations of the company, it approves big decisions, watches the chief executive and, if needed, replaces them. It’s designed to solve something economists call the “principal-agent problem”. A company’s managers (the agents) may put their own interests ahead of the owners’ (the principals). That’s why independence matters. Independent directors don’t work for the company and have no close financial or personal ties to its management. Filling a board with the chief executive’s employees (such as other senior executives) and friends is like letting students mark their own exams. Nvidia’s U-turn shows how fragile independence can be. A committee of independent directors is still investigating claims that Huang was targeted by China’s top spy agency. Huang is also due to answer questions from US lawmakers behind closed doors on December 1. The board brought him back before either had finished. The board acknowledged that its decision to rehire Huang was heavily influenced by the US government. It said it was “confident” Huang posed “no national security risk”, based on “input from senior US government levels”. We have seen other boards cave under pressure before. In November 2023, OpenAI’s board fired its chief executive, Sam Altman. Within days, nearly all of its 770 staff threatened to quit. Altman returned, and the board that sacked him was replaced. Independent of whom? On paper, there are strong safeguards to protect board independence. For example, the Nasdaq stock exchange, where Nvidia is listed, requires most directors to be independent. The committees that check a company’s accounts and set executive pay must be fully independent. But these rules fall short in three ways. First, the board itself gets to decide who counts as “independent”. In 2024, a US court found several Tesla directors who approved Elon Musk’s pay deal were too close to him to be independent. A higher court later restored the deal on other grounds. Second, directors get much of their information from the very executive team they are meant to be keeping in check. And third, a board without its own independent leader often struggles to push back against a chief executive. Nvidia only appointed its first-ever board chair on the day Huang resigned. Why no one should be irreplaceable “Key person” risk can’t be removed, but it can be managed. Boards can train a credible successor, appoint an independent chair before a crisis hits, and finish investigations before deciding. They should also explain their reasoning in public. An independent board that isn’t able to fire and replace a chief executive is just a cheer squad – not the umpire it’s supposed to be. This matters well beyond Silicon Valley. Many retirement funds around the world own shares in Nvidia. For the sake of protecting millions of people’s long-term savings, retirement funds and others representing shareholders should be advocating for better governance than we’ve seen at Nvidia so far. aa33fe05c91dcee3: Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”

The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”
HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company.
Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”
“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”

HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO said HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

Dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®

ec7b63860efa33d3: Malaysia Athletics cannot claim to have put its house in order while Karim Ibrahim remains president of one of its affiliates despite his disqualification by World Athletics.
Karim is not only the former president of Malaysia Athletics. He also heads Perak Athletics Association (Perak AA), a member of the national body.
MA’s endorsed constitution appears clear on the eligibility of people in such positions.

Article 13.2.8 bars anyone disqualified, removed or suspended by MA, the Olympic Council of Malaysia, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics or another local or international sports authority from being nominated, elected, appointed or holding office as an affiliate’s office-bearer, council member or committee member.
That restriction remains until the relevant authority lifts the sanction or the person succeeds in an appeal.

World Athletics has disqualified Karim. He has not appealed, and the sanction remains in force. The provision expressly covers office-holders in MA’s affiliates, not just those serving on its national executive council.

His position in Perak AA therefore puts MA’s responsibility to enforce its own constitution squarely in focus. The national body cannot leave the state association to decide whether it wishes to observe a rule that binds its members.
Affiliation carries obligations
MA’s authority to demand compliance rests on more than the eligibility provision.

Article 18.3 gives its constitution and by-laws precedence when they conflict with those of its members. Article 18.4 requires MA, its affiliates and people holding positions under its rules to comply with Malaysian law and the regulations of OCM, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics and other relevant international sports bodies.
Together, these clauses establish the obligations that come with membership. A state association cannot claim the benefits of affiliation while disregarding the rules governing the sport.
There is, however, a difference between requiring an affiliate to comply with MA’s constitution and automatically rewriting its registered rules.
If Perak AA’s constitution conflicts with the national one, it may still have to follow its own amendment procedures and the requirements of Malaysian law.

That does not excuse inaction. MA should formally notify Perak AA of the eligibility provision, explain its application and require the state body to address the position of its office-holders in accordance with the rules.

The same scrutiny should extend to every affiliate. MA must identify conflicting provisions or practices in state associations and set out what they need to do to comply. It should not wait for another dispute to expose weaknesses in its governance.
The council must be prepared to act
The executive council has a clear role in this process.

Article 18.1 gives it sole authority to interpret MA’s constitution and by-laws. Article 16.2 provides a mechanism for disputes between MA and its members, or between members. The council may seek OCM’s advice before making its final decision by majority.
These provisions give the council a way to resolve disagreements. They also place responsibility on it to address non-compliance.

That does not give the council licence to impose whatever penalty it chooses. It must identify the relevant breach, follow the proper procedures and give the affiliate a fair opportunity to respond. Any action must also comply with Malaysian law.
But procedural requirements should guide enforcement, not become an excuse to avoid it.

In Perak AA’s case, the council should establish the facts, determine the application of Article 13.2.8 and set out the steps needed to bring the state body into compliance. If Perak AA disputes the interpretation, the constitution provides a route to resolve the matter.

The same standards must apply to every affiliate. Perak AA should not receive special treatment because Karim once led the national association. Nor should any state body enjoy an exemption because of its influence or leadership.

This is not about stripping state associations of their autonomy. They should remain free to run their programmes, develop athletes and manage their affairs. But autonomy does not mean freedom to disregard the rules of the national and international sport.
The Karim episode exposed the consequences of a national body allowing its own rules to fall short of international requirements. MA must not allow that failure to continue at state level.
Its constitution gives it the authority to demand compliance. The executive council must now show that it has the resolve to use it.

3fa3cdca329aa8c5: Ironi adalah perkataan yang sepatutnya sinonim dengan politik. Apa tidaknya, musuh boleh jadi kawan, kawan boleh jadi musuh, orang yang ditentang reformasi dia pula yang memenangkannya.

Dulu tahun 80-an dan 90-an, saya menyokong Dr Mahathir Mohamad 100%. Kemudian saya amat membenci beliau dari tahun 1997 hingga 2016, berlatarkan reformasi ketika itu. Apabila beliau bekerjasama dengan Pakatan Harapan, saya menyokong Mahathir sehinggalah 2020 apabila beliau ditikam belakang oleh parti sendiri -- sedap juga melihat Mahathir ditikam oleh gengnya sendiri. Sekarang saya menulis pula bahawa pandangan beliau tentang PAS jelas lebih benar berbanding tanggapan saya terhadap parti itu, sejak dari 1997 hingga PAS berkawan dengan Umno dan Najib Razak.

Tujuan saya menulis artikel ini adalah kerisauan saya tentang nilai dan sikap orang Melayu. PAS kini memperlihatkan nilai yang cukup membimbangkan tetapi yang peliknya tak ramai agamawan akademik yang menegur secara langsung. Maka terpaksalah saya mencari orang yang orang Melayu hormat lebih daripada orang kerdil dalam politik seperti saya untuk memberi kesedaran tentang bahaya parti yang menunggang agama demi kuasa.

Baru-baru ini kita membaca tentang seorang pemimpin PAS yang mengatakan pemberian derma untuk membayar denda RM50 juta yang dikenakan ke atas seseorang yang didapati bersalah dalam kes penyelewengan dana adalah perbuatan yang dapat pahala. Sebelum ini, rasanya tahun lepas, PAS menjayakan tabung jihad untuk membayar saman fitnah untuk seorang wakil rakyatnya. Kedua-dua kes penyelewengan dana dan fitnah ini boleh kita telusur tanpa was-was. Kemudian, kita dapat tahu bahawa orang yang memfitnah serta orang yang pecah amanah dan salah guna kedudukan tidak menyatakan penyesalan, jauh lagi berikrar tidak akan mengulang lagi perbuatan.

Tidak cukup dengan itu, kita juga mendengar PAS menggunakan istilah munafik semasa membahaskan Belanjawan 2027 yang dibentangkan perdana menteri baru-baru ini. Ada pula presiden PAS menyifatkan Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan yang ditandatangani antara kerajaan dan beberapa Ahli Parlimen pembangkang sebagai pendekatan dajal. Kita sudah pun maklum tentang peristiwa membaca doa qunut nazilah terhadap orang yang tidak sehaluan dengan PAS. Isu mengkafirkan orang sudah pun tercatat dalam sejarah negara.
Maka itu saya menyingkap dua ucapan Mahathir dalam Perhimpunan Agung Umno pada 1984 dan 1999. Dalam ucapan 1984, Mahathir mengecam PAS seperti berikut;

"Umno adalah parti politik orang Melayu. Oleh kerana orang Melayu semuanya beragama Islam, maka Umno dengan sendirinya menjadi parti orang Islam Semenanjung Malaysia dan berjuang untuk agama Islam. Tetapi Umno bukan hipokrit dan berpura-pura menafikan yang ia adalah parti orang Melayu seperti yang dibuat oleh sebuah parti lain.

"Umno dengan jelas mengakui yang ianya parti kebangsaan Melayu di samping menjadi parti Islam. Menafi hakikat ini akan menjadikannya hipokrit atau munafik -- dan orang munafik tidak menjadi orang Islam yang jujur.

"Tidak ada cara yang lebih berkesan untuk mengekalkan kelemahan orang Melayu daripada menggunakan orang Melayu sendiri untuk melawan orang Melayu. Dengan tertubuhnya PAS maka terbentuklah alat utama musuh orang Melayu. Malang bagi mereka, kebanyakan daripada orang Melayu dapat meneka strategi pecah-belah ini dan telah terus menyokong Umno.

"Sekarang ini usaha ditumpukan kepada melemahkan semangat kebangsaan Melayu dengan mendakwa Islam menentang kebangsaan. Bahawa kebangsaan orang Melayu adalah satu alat mempertahankan diri bagi orang Melayu yang semuanya Islam, sama seperti kebangsaan Mujahidin mempertahankan orang Islam Afghanistan, dan tidak menjadi satu keangkuhan yang mengenepikan agama Islam dan orang Islam lain, tidak disebut. Mereka yang mendakwa bahawa mereka cuma mengakui keislaman mereka dan kononnya menolak semangat kebangsaan Melayu, tidak pula berani mempertahankan orang yang seagama dengan mereka di Afghanistan, atau di Lubnan atau di lain-lain tempat. Keislaman mereka terhad kepada kegiatan di Malaysia sahaja di mana kebangsaan Melayu Umno dapat memberi perlindungan kepada mereka. Sifat mereka ini adalah sifat hipokrit atau sifat talam dua muka. Dan mereka adalah begitu fanatik kepada parti mereka sehingga mereka tidak menyoal sama ada pendirian parti mereka baik atau tidak. Mereka inilah yang sebenarnya dari golongan asabiyah."
Jelas siapa sebenarnya hipokrit yang dimaksudkan Mahathir ketika itu. Namun demikian kita dapat merasai kesamaan mesej tersebut dalam tindak tanduk PAS ketika ini.

Dalam petikan kedua ucapan yang sama, Mahathir mempertikaikan PAS bahawa mereka sahaja yang tahu Islam manakala orang lain seperti Umno ketika itu yang juga mempunyai barisan pemimpin seperti Anwar Ibrahim tidak mencerminkan Islam sebenar.

"Sebagai satu lagi usaha untuk menentukan kejayaan orang Melayu, kita telah berusaha menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam. Kita tidak syak bahawa nilai-nilai Islam akan menjadikan orang Melayu orang yang lebih berjaya di dunia dan di akhirat. Pentadbiran yang diasaskan kepada nilai-nilai Islam tetap akan menjadi pentadbiran yang kukuh, adil dan berjaya.

"Di sini nilai-nilai Islam tidak bermakna rupa bentuk dan kebudayaan Arab yang menjadi tumpuan setengah-setengah orang Melayu di Malaysia. Memang benar rupa-bentuk boleh dijadikan simbol Islam dan ditiru dengan mudah. Tetapi rupa-bentuk tidak akan membawa kejayaan kepada kita. Yang akan membawa kejayaan ialah amalan nilai-nilai Islam seperti amanah, disiplin, taat setia, rajin dan tekun, bersaudara antara orang-orang mukmin, berani kerana benar, bertoleransi dan bertimbang rasa, adil, insaf dan syukur dan lain-lain lagi nilai yang mulia yang tidak begitu mudah diamal atau dipamerkan.

"Dalam ucapan saya di perhimpunan agung 1982, saya telah menjelaskan tentang hasrat kerajaan untuk menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam ke dalam pentadbiran negara. Maksud saya ialah supaya kita akan mentadbir dengan amanah, jujur, disiplin, setia, bertanggungjawab, cekap, bersih, dan lain-lain lagi nilai Islam yang akan menjadikan pentadbiran negara ini satu pentadbiran yang berkesan dan adil.

b879995cf1e26209: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

1479a2d5f1158c80: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

58c64dd3bfb5f2ac: In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges). We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness. A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles. But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls. “TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.” The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.  The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live. Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month. Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture. The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing. Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious. “The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.” A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life. Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.
e41a71b86838ecc4: Extraordinarily harsh droughts and heavy flooding have become more common around the globe this year due to an unusually strong El Niño. AP Photo/Charlie RiedelThe extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples. But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in. But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses. As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices. Gaps in climate science grow In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars. This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record. While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024. For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data. Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening. In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models. Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database. El Nino’s effects, especially strong in 2026, have disrupted crops and supply chains around the world, including a delayed monsoon season in India. Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images What this means for supply chains The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling. In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains. Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models. When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services. While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t. And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin. What it means for consumers Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves. Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year. And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026. A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth. 1e5a5d482e355f68: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.

That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.

As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of "dry hopping" (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.
