22995c289ab600a9: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide. The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted. Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights. Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya. The repatriation conundrum It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya. Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government. Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021. (AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko) Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament. This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility. The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army. The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region, where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state. The enforcement deficit The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided. But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law. Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it. The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs. How the ruling might help the Rohingya The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs. Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance. Read more: Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps. More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026. Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed. It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community. Not ‘illegal immigrants’ Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine. The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice. San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.
e2ba0e13f0a1a55f: In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families. “I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change. For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom. For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English. Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue. A country of 124 mother tongues Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, though the state has not always acknowledged it. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues. Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages. Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population. I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity. The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities. In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language, a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali. For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue. Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011. Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk. Rights on paper On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues. In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown, policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support. In a 2026 study from Tanahun, one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.” Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013. (Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID), CC BY The evidence for local languages A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams. Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English, according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale. In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.” Obstacles to implementation A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents, points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.” Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained. Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget, well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education. Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them. From paper to practice As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.” Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities. Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues. Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they. Mark Turin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC).

89de79cca67002c9: DENIS ESAULOV 1987/ShutterstockThe recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems. It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda. Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers. Ending unanimity Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap. In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting). Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters. So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions. A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets. The Cop climate negotiation process hinges on all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. metamorworks/Shutterstock It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend). It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration (issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business. Coalition of the willing Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?” This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks. Read more: What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results. As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute. The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero). We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats. Francesco Grillo is Director of the think tank Vision.

Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You’ll Be the Main Character

Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.

Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The and parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”

It suggests that the channel would be connected to an “advertising server,” and that advertisements would be inserted into the customized AI content: “an advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item,” it says.

The patent imagines, for example, “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience” with a viewer named “John” as the protagonist. Another prompt included in the patent suggests that someone who had recently watched cricket highlights of a “Player 1” might then be served a similar video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.”

The notable thing about this patent is that it is barely an evolution of what is already happening on social media and what is beginning to happen on streaming free TV channels on services like Samsung TV Plus and TCLtv+.

The people generating AI slop on social media are making incredibly specific content because they know that social media algorithms will be highly effective at filtering people there. Meta is already allowing advertisers to use AI to generate many slightly different versions of an advertisement; its targeting AI then automatically shows them to users who are most likely to react to a specific version of an ad. As I’ve previously reported, TCL has been experimenting with AI-generated content on its streaming free TV channels, and, even without AI-generated content, free streaming TV channels have gotten incredibly specific. It is now possible, for example, to watch reruns of individual shows 24/7/365.

AI boosters have long been saying the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own TV shows, or to generate “new” episodes of existing properties. An always-on, autogenerating, customized AI TV channel isn’t far off from that idea.

As I’ve previously argued, the future that tech companies envision is one in which we are somehow even more siloed than we are now. They imagine a world in which everyone lives in their own reality and watches their own, customized content, which is a world in which big, unifying pieces of media are harder to make and are few and far between. The Google patent comes on the heels of a Microsoft patent that describes a system that alters spoken words (and the person’s lips) in live video, thereby distorting reality.

University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight On: Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

University of Michigan Mailer Promises Its Data Center Isn’t Really a Data Center: And, related, over the past month, the University of Michigan sent postcards and pamphlets to people in Michigan telling them its new data center is “NOT a commercial data center” and is, instead, a “research computing center.” According to one of the postcards viewed by 404 Media, the University’s data center will “advance breakthrough research in medicine, clean energy, cybersecurity, and engineering,” and "accelerate discoveries like new drug therapies and cancer treatments that improve people’s lives.” The University's postcard also promised to create 300 “high-quality union jobs during development” and “preserve approximately 80% of the 124-acre property as green space.”

The biggest story in the tech world is, once again, Nvidia and the Jensen Huang scandal. Outside of mentioning it in this newsletter, we haven’t really been covering this. The main reason is that these are one of the few types of stories that we’re not really set up to do. Nvidia is technically the most valuable company on the planet, and so other bigger news outlets have a bunch of reporters who are dedicated to covering just Nvidia. When a scandal like this breaks, they throw entire news teams at it. It just doesn’t really make sense for us to try to compete with our smaller team. The New York Times, Bloomberg, The Information, and the Wall Street Journal (and lots of other outlets) are all over this. It does feel bad to more or less sit out such a big news story, and it’s not that we don’t think this scandal is important. It’s just that we are usually trying to break new ground, and it’s hard to do that when hundreds of other reporters are laser focused on the same scandal. We reserve the right to jump in at any time, especially with a reported take or something like this. I do think it’s depressing that this has become a culture war thing, and an opportunity for Silicon Valley VCs and billionaires to do class solidarity and try to show that there should be no consequences whatsoever for bad behaving CEOs. I think the Trump and essentially stock market by blackmail aspect of it all is quite worrisome, too. Huang’s return raises all sorts of national security concerns, corruption concerns, and questions about how (much more) subservient Huang will be to Trump now that he’s done him a massive favor. I also found this exchange to be upsetting on many levels. Also, this post from Balaji, one of the worst to ever do it, is wildly deranged and will probably make your blood boil. Anyways, that’s enough of that for the moment. Here’s what else is going on.
cd73b5dbfdcc46aa: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Over the past month, the University of Michigan sent postcards and pamphlets to people in Michigan telling them its new data center is “NOT a commercial data center” and is, instead, a “research computing center.”

According to one of the postcards viewed by 404 Media, the University’s data center will “advance breakthrough research in medicine, clean energy, cybersecurity, and engineering,” and "accelerate discoveries like new drug therapies and cancer treatments that improve people’s lives.” The University's postcard also promised to create 300 “high-quality union jobs during development” and “preserve approximately 80% of the 124-acre property as green space.”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> One of U of M’s mailers said the building will not operate as a commercial data center. “This facility will not support streaming, entertainment, social media, or e-commerce,” it said. It also said the facility will not “burden the local community with the cost of its energy or water use, drain resources from the local community or raise utility rates,” or “create smoke, odors, or significant noise.”

The University has said it’s not sure how much water the data center will use but that it could be as much as 650,000 gallons a day. It also said it’s “evaluating several cooling techniques to identify the most efficient approach,” a process that “includes continued evaluation of reclaimed wastewater for cooling, which would significantly reduce demand on municipal potable water supply systems.”

Los Alamos National Labs (LANL), America’s nuclear weapons scientists, have partnered with the U of M to construct a massive $1.2 billion 290,000 square-foot data center in Ypsilanti, Township, Michigan. Residents of the Township are angry about the “research computing center” and worry about how much water it’ll use, what it’ll do to electricity bills, and its connection to nuclear weapons.

In April, the Township’s utilities authority approved a moratorium on delivering water to data center projects while it studied how they might impact the community’s water supply. In response, U of M sent a letter to the Township utility board threatening legal action.

Concerned Township residents have spent the past year strategizing with community leaders about how to delay or stop construction. The Township’s anger caught U of M off guard and it attempted to address community concerns in several public meetings. It hasn’t gone well.

The pamphlet attempted to contextualize the data center’s place in America’s nuclear weapons research. “It would not involve nuclear weapons manufacturing, physical weapons testing, or the storage of hazardous nuclear materials,” the pamphlet said. But it would help “improve cybersecurity practices to safely manage existing nuclear material out of state.” In January, LANL confirmed its portion of the data center would be used for nuclear weapons research.
U of M did not return 404 Media’s request for comment.

On November 19, the board of regents approved the next phase of development for the data center in a vote of 7-1. The same night, Ypsilanti Township hosted a panel discussion about the data center where its leaders promised to continue to fight. “We have a number of strategies right now that we’re going to be pursuing,” Township attorney Douglas Winters said at the panel. “We believe that U of M has gone far afield when it comes to the constitutional autonomy which they have enjoyed by virtue of being a university.”

Masters in Business Transcript: David Eichhorn, CEO and Head of Investment Strategies, NISA Investment Advisors
[00:00:02] ANNOUNCER: Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news.

David Eichhorn has been CEO there for a few years, as well as the head of investment strategies. He’s not just a fixed income and pension fund investor, he’s a quant. I thought this conversation was fascinating and I think you will too. With no further ado, my conversation with NISA’s David Eichhorn. David Eichhorn, welcome to Bloomberg.
[00:01:09] DAVID EICHHORN: Barry, I’m delighted to be here. Love the show, and excited to chat today.

[00:01:13] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m delighted to have you. What you guys do is really fascinating and so unusual. We’re going to delve into that. Was that it from the start?

[00:01:41] DAVID EICHHORN: Mostly the career plan was, you know, pay bills, honestly, and try to work through school and all that. But yeah, I’ve always considered myself a quant at heart, and so it was a really nice and fortunate combination. I’d love to say there was a great plan in it, but I’m a first-generation college grad. I didn’t know that was even a thing until some number of years ago, when it became popular to talk about that.
[00:02:04] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Right. First one in your family to go to college?

[00:02:06] DAVID EICHHORN: No, all my brothers and sisters, but our generation was the first. And so it certainly was great being local at Washington University. I grew up in St. Louis. I was a commuter, which isn’t even allowed anymore. Probably a regrettable decision from a college life experience. But I had to work a lot to pay the bills at Wash U, when it was still possible to pay for college. Still, back then. But the math really was the superpower that I think supercharged the finance degree, frankly.

So I met Phil Dybvig, who I love to describe now as Nobel Laureate Phil Dybvig, at Washington University. Because of the math degree, he took a shine to me, for lack of a better term. And it’s one of those—in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king. I had some programming background. I knew relatively sophisticated math for what was in the finance department, and he really helped get me my first job at JP Morgan. And I’m eternally grateful for Phil, and he remains a great friend to this day.

[00:03:07] BARRY RITHOLTZ: You spent your first three years after college at JP Morgan, again working on the institutional side, helping clients develop investment policies, strategic asset allocations, and perhaps most importantly, asset-liability management strategies. Tell us about your JP Morgan experience.

[00:03:26] DAVID EICHHORN: Well, I’ll probably come back to the theme many times, but serendipity has struck a lot in my career. So Phil connected me with Mike Granito at JP Morgan, who ran what they called the Strategic Investment Advisory Group. I dumb-lucked into that. That was a group of, I think at the time, 17 or 18 PhDs. A couple of us were the first-ever undergrad hires, and even within that group, I lucked into—as opposed to cleansing databases and doing awful work that the quants needed—I somehow got put in a client-facing role very quickly. We shared free consulting, maybe in air quotes, free consulting, to our large clients: classic mean-variance optimization-style analysis of managers, things that were newer for the time to roll out to clients. And so I got a great background in that.

And at that time, while most people weren’t doing it, we started really pushing the concept of asset-liability management, really what became, I’d say, the forerunner to LDI-type strategies. How do you—amongst other things, but certainly for large corporate pensions—how do you manage risk, as opposed to in an absolute context, how do you manage it vis-à-vis liability, whether that be how you think about your equity allocation, but maybe most importantly how you think about your fixed income allocation? How does it mitigate some of the liability’s inherent interest rate risk? And again, not many people listened in the late nineties, and that kind of continued on into the early aughts at NISA. But it was setting the groundwork for what ultimately became known as LDI.

[00:04:57] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And so I think the average layperson hears “liability” and they’re thinking car accident. Explain, especially from a pension fund manager’s perspective, what do future liabilities mean in plain English?

[00:05:10] DAVID EICHHORN: Well, our industry uses some funny terminology, like liability. It is a liability. Ultimately the corporation—I kind of think of it a little differently. It’s a promise by the corporation to its participants and its employees to pay them a benefit in the future. And of course, there are a lot of rules around these promises and how to fund them over time, because of a lot of issues that have occurred in past decades. So these are pension trusts where assets are set aside to pay off, quote, these liabilities. But what the liability represents is pensions that have been very much earned by the participants, who are owed a retirement benefit—typically classic defined benefit structures, a retirement benefit for life when you’ve retired, often with some portion of it that will outlive you if your spouse outlives you, et cetera. So they’re very long-dated, really bonds effectively.

And that’s kind of what we wanted to point out. Certainly in our early days at NISA, we were pointing out these liabilities and pension funds—think of it as a short position in a bond. You owe someone money for a long, long time. So if interest rates fall, that makes that liability more valuable, i.e., all else equal, harder to pay off. And if interest rates go up, vice versa. So a natural mitigation strategy is to own bonds, own very long bonds like zero-coupon Treasury strips. That was some of our early innovation at NISA. And then over time, as folks got more and more comfortable with derivative strategies, using things like Treasury futures, interest rate swaps, a whole host of things, to hedge more and more of that interest rate risk with a derivative instrument to offset the volatility of that liability.
[00:06:48] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And there’s a quote of yours that I found.
[00:06:53] DAVID EICHHORN: Okay. I say way too much, so who knows. What did I say?

[00:07:07] DAVID EICHHORN: Yes. It’s what I tell our new hires all the time. And I always say that because it’s funny—work a lot of hours, invest a lot of your time, just work a lot, work really hard right out of school, comma, says the CEO, right? 0fc51390fa9c3aee: About half a million Californians were affected by the state's hike in minimum wage for fast-food workers. AP Photo/Jae C. HongEven before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries. As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results. In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate. As a researcher of health and labor markets, I joined with economists David Neumark, Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs. We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at. For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%. This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain. The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own. Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase. Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own. In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027. With the federal minimum wage unchanged since 2009, many states and municipalities have raised the wage floor on their own, including for specific sectors. AP Photo/Andrew Harnik Smaller chains see an impact The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists. In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero. More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run. Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage? We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures. We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones. For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period. But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose. How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones. A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses. Taking the longer view First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%. That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains. Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage. For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear. Liam Sigaud is affiliated with the Paragon Health Institute, a not-for-profit health policy research organization.

84edfb5a38475599: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

Today marks exactly 10 years since Amri Che Mat went missing.
A Suhakam public inquiry unanimously concluded in 2019 that Amri was a victim of enforced disappearance – specifically by state agents, namely the police's Special Branch.
It was past 11pm on Nov 24, 2016, a Thursday, when Amri drove out of his house at Padang Behor in Kangar, Perlis, to have supper with a friend.
Just minutes later, less than a kilometre from his house, his Toyota Fortuner was boxed in by three four-wheel-drives. Screeching sounds, glass breaking, and that was it. It took less than a minute.
Providence would have it that the incident was witnessed by a passing motorcyclist and a restaurant owner across the road from where it happened.

Amri’s Fortuner was found abandoned at a construction site in Bukit Chabang, Kedah, a few hours later. His wife, Norhayati Ariffin, did not realise Amri hadn't come home until the next morning when she received a call about the abandoned car.
Before Amri took a nap at 7.30pm, he had asked his wife to wake him up at 10.30pm. That was the last time Norhayati saw her husband.
This sounds like a bad conspiracy novel, but reality is stranger than fiction.

DNA swabs were taken from the Fortuner when the car was found, but were sent to the chemistry department only five months later. Amri’s family also did not get the police support they wanted. Instead of trying to locate Amri, Norhayati was queried about her husband’s involvement in Shia activities.
Shia Islam is prohibited in Malaysia and Amri was watched by religious authorities and the police, but was never arrested or charged. Instead, he disappeared.
How do we know Amri was being watched? Would he have disappeared at a different time if he didn’t go out that fateful night? It's quite possible judging by the circumstances.
A car workshop owner across Amri’s house later testified that unknown cars, with engines running, took turns parking outside Amri's house day and night for three days before he went missing.
One of those cars was a gold-coloured Toyota Vios with a Penang number plate, which was also spotted when Pastor Raymond Koh was abducted 81 days later.

The Vios belonged to an operative of the Special Branch in Kuala Lumpur. He was identified as Saiful Bahari Abdul Aziz, but the police always had an excuse for why the key witness could not be present to testify.
Koh was abducted the same way on Feb 13, 2017. His car was also boxed in as men in black rushed out from three black four-wheel-drives. There was also a gold-coloured Vios nearby.

Koh’s abduction was more audacious than Amri’s; it happened in broad daylight on a Monday morning in SS4, Petaling Jaya. Amri’s case only had eyewitness accounts but Koh's case included video evidence.
Besides witness Roeshan Celestine Gomez, a chambering student who happened to be driving behind Koh's car, the pastor's abduction was caught on the CCTV cameras of two houses nearby.

Strangely, the police didn’t rush to get the CCTV recordings. It was Koh’s family who looked for them once they knew about Roeshan’s police report. After the CCTV recordings were spread through the media, the case couldn't be hidden any longer.

With two Malaysians abducted this way – and Joshua Helmi and Ruth Sitepu also missing since end-November 2016 – and a growing suspicion they were abducted, a group of civil society groups sent a memo to Suhakam seeking action.

Suhakam then carried out public inquiries on both Koh and Amri’s disappearances. Amri’s case took Suhakam 10 months to complete starting from January 2018, with 27 days of hearings and 24 witnesses summoned.

Suhakam's final reports said evidence pointed to Amri and Koh being forcibly abducted by the Special Branch. It also stated that in both cases, the police failed to investigate the disappearances properly.

The Cabinet then set up a special task force in 2019 to look into the matter. Its report in 2020 stated that it was “highly probable that Amri’s disappearance was caused by rogue police officers acting alone or in a group with unidentified individuals from religious groups".

Three years after Amri disappeared, Norhayati, who became a single mother to their four daughters, sued the police and government for malfeasance and failure to investigate his abduction properly, among others.

The civil suit filed on Nov 18, 2019, took six years, partly because the government initially refused to release the special task force's report. By the time the High Court made its decision, nine years had passed since Amri disappeared.

On Nov 5, 2025, the High Court awarded Norhayati general and exemplary damages totalling RM3 million, and another RM14,457.52 mainly for the children’s education expenses. The court also ordered a re-investigation into Amri’s disappearance.

Justice Su Tiang Joo said the police breached their own SOPs, citing severe delays in handling DNA evidence, failure to investigate the Vios owner, and failure to investigate CCTV recordings, among others. The police also made almost no effort to keep the family updated.

Su said Norhayati’s mental anguish, pain and suffering included having to dissolve her marriage under fasakh – as advised by the Perlis religious affairs department – “to bring succour to the needs of the four daughters".

Norhayati was unable to get welfare aid as a single mother if she remained married to Amri. Secondly, the divorce dispensed of the need for Amri to be a wali for one of their daughters who was getting married.
Perhaps it was to be expected that the attorney-general would appeal the High Court decision. With that, the award was stayed while Norhayati and her daughters continue to wait.
Today, we want to remember Amri.
Whatever wrongs he allegedly committed, Amri deserves a fair chance at defending himself in a court of law.
That’s the basic minimum of a modern democratic society proclaiming the supremacy of the constitution and rule of law as two of its five Rukun Negara tenets.

Abducting Amri was cowardly and dastardly because the government has the machinery, laws, institutions and manpower resources to frame a legal case against him and prosecute him, if he indeed did wrong.
The police chose a shortcut instead, and the executive arm of the government allowed that shortcut. This was a betrayal of the rakyat's trust.
Today, we remember Amri Che Mat, a Malaysian, a father of four girls (now grown women), and surely, a friend to many through his NGO, Perlis Hope.
Ann Teoh is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
9c8bf06abbbe421e: Complaints include marriage disputes, unfair trial, unlawful land grabs, corruption, torture, and more
Originally published on Global Voices
An old man in the Talas province addressing Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov during a public meeting. Photo from the Presidential Administration's website. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In October and November 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sadyr Japarov, held public meetings with the population in all seven provinces of the country. What were meant to be formal events turned into quests for justice by people driven to desperation.
The meetings revealed the ineffectiveness of the existing justice mechanisms and showed how people saw the president as the only guarantor of justice.

The effectiveness of Kyrgyzstan’s law enforcement and judicial bodies was people’s most common justice-related complaint. During a meeting with residents of the southwestern Batken province on October 11, a woman complained to the president about her former husband, who accused her of forging their marriage certificate and framed her for crimes she did not commit to avoid the division of assets after their divorce.

She also said her former brother-in-law provided false testimony to back up his brother’s accusations. She now lives in an apartment with their three children in constant fear that her former husband may kick them out because he allegedly bribed police and courts.

This trivial legal dispute reached the point where the woman had to beg the president to ensure a just investigation and ruling. Japarov condemned her former husband and said that he should have left everything to her and their kids after the divorce.
Here is an Instagram reel with his response to the case.
View this post on Instagram

On October 26, Japarov met with residents of the Kazarman district in the southern Jalalabad province, where Shirimbek Abrahmanov told the president about his father, who was imprisoned for allegedly offering a bribe of KGS 2,000 (USD 23) to a police officer during a traffic stop. The district court acquitted him of the charges.
However, the local prosecutor’s office appealed the decision in the provincial court, which found Abdrahmanov’s father guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison.
Here is an Instagram reel with the complaint and Japarov’s response.
View this post on Instagram
Japarov could not hide his anger when he heard the story, especially after finding out the provincial court took seven months to issue a verdict. In reply, he confronted local authorities and said:

Are the traffic police officer and the prosecutor in cahoots? Does that mean they’ve ganged up on him? If it were a large bribe, that would be one thing. But to have someone imprisoned over two thousand soms — that’s a disgrace.
The man was released from custody shortly after Japarov’s intervention and subsequent pardon.
Similar complaints resurfaced multiple times during presidential meetings in other provinces, highlighting systemic problems plaguing the judicial and law-enforcement systems.
The message is clear: people have lost all hope of finding justice at the hands of local police and courts.

Surprisingly, following his meetings with the public, Japarov concluded that the level of distrust towards courts has decreased, but admitted that problems in the judicial system remain and must be solved quickly.

On the one hand, the lack of justice and the dysfunction within the courts and police bodies, which are plagued by corruption and bureaucracy, are real pressing issues affecting millions of people across Kyrgyzstan. However, the current political regime led by Japarov, who came to power in October 2020, has made little tangible progress.
In 2026, Kyrgyzstan was ranked 99th out of 144 states in the Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project. For comparison, in 2020, it was ranked 87th.

On the other hand, people’s desperate appeals for justice helped Japarov sustain his man-of-the-people image. By listening to people’s requests and swiftly resolving their issues, the president can reinforce his popularity. In turn, this leads to the maintenance of the personalistic regime built around Japarov since his arrival to power.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

Nikos Oikonomou/Anadolu via Getty ImagesThe International Court of Justice (ICJ) last week ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority group. The court found Myanmar breached its obligations under the United Nations genocide convention to prevent and punish genocide. This ruling is not just important for the Rohingya and Myanmar. It may also have a significant legal impact on other genocide cases before the court – in particular, South Africa’s case alleging Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Other genocide cases Four cases currently before the ICJ concern allegations of breaches of the genocide convention. One was brought by Ukraine against Russia following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Another was brought by Nicaragua against Germany, regarding Germany’s support of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The third was brought by the Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwanda, which includes claims about Rwanda’s involvement in conflict in the Kivu provinces of the DRC. The Myanmar ruling may have repercussions for all these cases. However, the judgement will mostly affect the fourth genocide case before the court, the one brought by South Africa against Israel. Multiple intents Genocide is different from “ordinary” crimes in that it requires a “special intent” (or dolus specialis) – the intent to destroy a national, racial, ethnic or religious group, in whole or in part. This must be proven in addition to a general criminal intent, where a perpetrator intends to commit the crime or could have foreseen the result of their actions. Genocidal intent is proven by two main forms of evidence. Firstly, there are the statements of political and military leaders, soldiers, the media and key figures in society. These often dehumanise the targeted group and may explicitly refer to the destruction of the group in some way. The second way intent is proven is by looking at the perpetrators’ pattern of conduct. In the Myanmar case, the court considered hate speech by Myanmar authorities against the Rohingya to be incitement to genocide. This formed evidence of intent. The judges also used the military’s pattern of conduct to determine intent. Myanmar argued its intent was a counterinsurgency operation against a terrorist group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA). But the court determined the conduct of Myanmar’s security forces did not align with an intent to carry out a genuine counterinsurgency operation. The court held that acts such killing civilians (including children), raping women, and destroying villages did not form part of legitimate military operations – even if the operation also had the intent of meeting military objectives. This is significant for the Israel genocide case because Israel argues it is fighting in self-defence in Gaza against a terrorist group, Hamas. However, statements from Israeli government ministers about the intention to deny Palestinians necessities of life, or to erase Palestine from the map, may suggest a different intent. As in the Myanmar case, the violence in Gaza has included the killing of civilians (including children), the widespread destruction of buildings (including in residential areas), and sexual and gender-based violence. The Myanmar judgement gives the court an opening to decide that Israel has had both an intent to fight Hamas and a genocidal intent. Or it could decide Israel’s operations in Gaza do not represent a legitimate and lawful way to carry out an anti-terrorism military operation, which may demonstrate clear genocidal intent. Killing of children One of the key aspects of The Gambia’s case against Myanmar was that the killing of children demonstrated genocidal intent. The reason: killing children is not a legitimate military objective. The ICJ agreed. The court held that the killing of up to 2,000 children under the age of five was a significant indicator that Myanmar intended to destroy the future of the Rohingya people. According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, Israel has killed almost 22,000 children under 18 in Gaza. Some have been killed in indiscriminate attacks. Others have been deliberately targeted, according to the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel. Following the court’s Myanmar decision, the killing of so many children in Gaza may strengthen the case against a legitimate military operation, and that the military and therefore the state instead had genocidal intent. Broader context of crimes The Myanmar cased focused on the so-called “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in 2017. However, this violence was placed in the context of a lengthy history of discrimination and persecution of the Rohingya. The court recognised that violations of human rights, which may not necessarily amount to genocidal crimes, were part of the bigger picture of the genocide. The exclusion of the Rohingya from citizenship was one example, as it denied them access to education, employment, healthcare, food and free movement. Similarly, South Africa’s case against Israel positions the violence in Gaza since 2023 as an escalating step in decades of discrimination and persecution – a system of apartheid – against Palestinians. Scale and targeting of crimes ICJ judges also recognised that the scale of the crimes in Myanmar was relevant to the finding that genocide occurred, alongside the fact the violence specifically targeted the Rohingya. Thousands of Rohingya were killed and raped, and myriad Rohingya villages were destroyed. Non-Rohingya were not attacked, and their villages were not burned. This has parallels to the situation in Gaza. Large numbers of Palestinians have been killed and injured, and huge swathes of Gaza have been destroyed. It is estimated it will take many years and billions of dollars to clear and rebuild Gaza. These findings have clear parallels with the situation in Gaza, and will undoubtedly be drawn on by South Africa as its case against Israel progresses in the coming years. d72fc07dea2532a0: Hari itu Ahmad Maslan berpantun di Dewan Rakyat. Selain terkenal dengan resipi nasi gorengnya, Timbalan menteri kerja raya itu memang gemar berpantun. Tapi, bukan tentang kenapa dan apa sebab beliau berpantun yang ingin saya ceritakan. Tolak ke tepi bab politik, saya rasa ada sesuatu yang wajar kita hargai daripada kegemaran beliau itu. Bagi saya pantun perlu diangkat sebagai pusaka negara dan mesti diajar dengan serius di sekolah ketika kita mencari formula lain dalam usaha menggalakkan pelajar berfikir secara kritis dan kreatif.

Pantun mampu mengasah kemahiran tersebut. Hari ini tak ramai orang mampu berpantun secara spontan. Kalau diberikan pen dan kertas serta masa setengah jam, mungkin ramai yang boleh menghasilkan pantun empat kerat. Itupun pantun yang asal boleh sajalah! Bukan pantun yang betul-betul bermutu tinggi. Tetapi bagaimana jika kita perlu melakukannya dalam masa beberapa saat atau membalas pantun secara spontan? Saya percaya kita memang gagal. Di situlah menariknya pantun sebagai penajam akal.

Kita selalu membicarakan pantun sebagai warisan kesusasteraan Melayu. Tetapi jarang sekali kita membicarakannya dari sudut keupayaan kognitif manusia. Bagi saya, pantun bukan sekadar permainan bahasa, tetapi juga suatu bentuk latihan ketangkasan berfikir. Bayangkan apa yang berlaku dalam kepala seseorang ketika mencipta pantun secara spontan. Kita perlu memikirkan perkara yang hendak disampaikan, mencari perkataan yang sesuai, menyusun ayat, memadankan rima serta membina pembayang. Semua itu dilakukan hampir serentak. Belum lagi kalau pantun itu perlu dijawab apabila ada yang menjualnya.

Otak perlu bekerja untuk memahami maksud yang disampaikan oleh orang lain, merumuskan jawapan dan menterjemahkan jawapan itu dalam bentuk puisi yang mempunyai peraturan tertentu. Ini bukan mudah. Cuma, selama ini kita lihat pantun seolah-olah dipermainkan dan dijadikan bahan lawak sahaja dalam rancangan hiburan atau persembahan komedi. Kita kena serius sekali-sekala.

Dalam bidang pendidikan, kita sering bercakap tentang pemikiran kritis. Kita mahu anak-anak kita mempunyai kemampuan menganalisis, mentafsir, membuat perkaitan dan menyelesaikan masalah secara kreatif. Menariknya, sebahagian daripada kemahiran berfikir itu sudah lama dilatih oleh nenek moyang kita melalui suatu kegiatan yang hari ini sering kita anggap sekadar hiburan.

Bukanlah bermaksud syarat hendak berpantun mestilah mempunyai pemikiran kritis yang tinggi. Tetapi proses mencipta pantun itu sendiri memerlukan beberapa kemahiran mental yang amat berguna dalam membentuk pemikiran seseorang. Pantun juga ada tingkatannya. Ada pantun yang mudah, sekadar memadankan bunyi di hujung baris. Ada pula pantun yang pembayangnya mempunyai hubungan makna dengan maksud yang hendak disampaikan. Lebih tinggi lagi apabila pencipta pantun menggunakan perlambangan alam untuk menyampaikan falsafah kehidupan. Contohnya pantun ini:-
Yang kurik itu kundi, Yang merah itu saga; Yang baik itu budi, Yang indah itu bahasa.

Betapa ekonomisnya penggunaan bahasa dalam menyampaikan suatu pemikiran. Tak perlu panjang berjela, empat baris sahaja sudah cukup untuk membicarakan nilai kemanusiaan. Orang Melayu dahulu memerhatikan alam. Mereka melihat tumbuh-tumbuhan, haiwan, sungai, laut dan perubahan cuaca. Daripada pemerhatian itu, mereka membina perlambangan dan menghubungkannya dengan kehidupan manusia. Ini bukan sekadar persoalan penguasaan bahasa. Ini juga persoalan keupayaan membuat perkaitan antara dua perkara yang pada zahirnya kelihatan tidak mempunyai hubungan. Kemampuan membuat perkaitan inilah yang dimaksudkan sebagai salah satu ciri pemikiran kreatif.

Menteri pendidikan patut beri perhatian yang serius akan kemahiran yang sudah lama kita miliki ini. Pantun bukan sekadar diajar sebagai salah satu bentuk puisi tradisional dalam mata pelajaran bahasa Melayu semata-mata tetapi dijadikan kegiatan yang melatih anak-anak berfikir secara spontan. Adakan sesi jual beli pantun di dalam kelas. Seorang pelajar mengemukakan persoalan dalam bentuk pantun dan seorang lagi menjawabnya juga dalam bentuk pantun. Biarkan mereka belajar sambil berseronok walaupun pada permulaannya mungkin mutu pantun masih rendah. Lama-kelamaan sudah tentu pelajar akan jadi mahir serta tangkas seperti pantun lama ini:
Limau purut lebat di pangkal, Batang mengkudu condong uratnya; Hujan ribut dapat ditangkal, Hati yang rindu apa ubatnya?

Perhatikan kehalusannya. Jika anak-anak kita mampu mencipta pantun sebegini bermakna mereka telah memahami falsafah hubungan perasaan manusia dengan fenomena alam. Hujan ribut yang dahsyat sekalipun masih dianggap mampu ditangkal, tetapi kerinduan yang tidak kelihatan itu belum tentu mampu diubati.

Bayangkan juga jika seorang guru sains meminta anak muridnya menerangkan sesuatu konsep sains melalui pantun. Sudahlah perlu memahami konsep itu, mereka perlu pula memikirkan cara menyampaikannya dalam empat baris. Tentulah ada yang secara sinis mempersoalkan mengapa perlu menyusahkan diri sedangkan penerangan biasa lebih mudah. Inilah yang saya maksudkan sejak awal lagi ia bertujuan untuk mencabar kemampuan minda. Contoh lucunya ialah mamat-mamat sado yang mengangkat besi di gimnasium pun boleh kita tanyakan soalan yang sama. Mengapa bersusah payah mengangkat besi berat sebab lepas itu letak semula besi tersebut di tempat asalnya. Tapi kita segera faham yang dia sedang melatih ototnya, manakala orang yang berpantun pula sedang melatih akalnya.

Dalam zaman kecerdasan buatan hari ini, kita boleh meminta komputer menghasilkan puluhan pantun dalam beberapa saat. Tetapi tujuan mengajar anak-anak berpantun bukanlah semata-mata untuk mendapatkan pantun yang indah. Yang lebih penting ialah proses mental yang dilalui untuk menghasilkan pantun tersebut. Kita tidak mahu sekadar melahirkan generasi yang tahu mendapatkan jawapan. Kita juga mahu melahirkan generasi yang tahu bagaimana hendak berfikir untuk mendapatkan jawapan. Bertuahnya kita ialah kita sudah ada kaedah yang praktikal dalam hal ini tetapi kita kesampingkannya. Orang tua kita dulu apabila berpantun macam, GhatGpt. Prompt saja terus keluar jawapan.

Satu lagi keistimewaan pantun ialah kemampuannya menyampaikan teguran secara halus. Orang boleh berselisih pendapat, menyindir, menegur, malah berbahas tanpa semestinya menggunakan bahasa yang kasar. Dalam zaman manusia begitu mudah memaki hamun di media sosial, alangkah menariknya jika mereka perlu berpantun dahulu sebelum mahu bergaduh. Sekurang-kurangnya ada tapisan sedikit sebelum menghina orang. Kedengaran mungkin lucu, tapi kita lihatlah hari ini berapa ramai mengalami kemurungan akibat dimaki hamun di media sosial. Barangkali ada yang akan membatalkan hasrat untuk bergaduh kerana terlalu sibuk mencari pembayang. Lihatlah ketika Ahmad Maslan berpantun. Bunyinya tenang sahaja tetapi 'makan dalam'. Berbanding beberapa Ahli Parlimen yang gemar menjerit dan bertempik sehingga penyokong sendiri pun naik malu.

Kita patut berbangga dengan warisan budaya kita. Namun, kebanggaan itu tidak seharusnya terhenti pada usaha memelihara bentuknya semata-mata. Kita juga harus menggali kebijaksanaan di sebalik penciptaannya dan mencari bagaimana ia boleh dimanfaatkan dalam kehidupan moden. Pantun bukan sekadar khazanah bahasa. Ia juga khazanah pemikiran. Nenek moyang kita bukan sahaja mewariskan keindahan berbahasa, malah suatu kaedah untuk melatih ketangkasan akal.

Kalau kita sendiri kurang menghargai keistimewaan pantun, tahukah kita bahawa hampir dua abad dahulu sasterawan Perancis sudah tertarik dengannya? Pada tahun 1829, Victor Hugo, pengarang Les Misérables, memperkenalkan pantun berkait Melayu menerusi antologi puisinya, Les Orientales. Bentuk puisi ini kemudian diadaptasi oleh penyair Perancis sehingga dikenali sebagai pantoum.

Bayangkan, ketika orang Eropah sedang meneroka keunikan struktur puisi warisan kita, nenek moyang kita sudah menjadikannya sebahagian daripada cara mereka berkomunikasi dalam kehidupan seharian. Sayang sekali jika kita hanya mewarisi pantunnya tetapi tidak mewarisi kecerdasan berfikir yang melahirkan pantun itu. Dan dalam bab ini, saya menghargai kegemaran Ahmad Maslan berpantun. Agak-agak bernas atau tidak cadangan saya agar kemahiran berpantun diajar secara serius di sekolah?
