402e4abf38c942a1: In South Asia, survivors of sexual and physical abuse are often met with judgment and stigma
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.
Editorial note: This article contains mention of gender-based violence, sexual assault, violence against children, and child sexual abuse, which may be triggering for some readers.

November 25 to December 10, 2026, marks the UN’s 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence. However, even as gender-based violence gets more recognition globally, survivors are still struggling to access social or legal justice. South Asia is no exception to this. Global Voices sat down with one survivor of childhood abuse who uses her experience to fuel her advocacy work today.

South Asia is home to nearly one quarter of the world’s population, woven with a diverse, culture-driven fabric where women are often celebrated as goddesses. However, this veneration doesn’t necessarily mean South Asian women are safe or free from abuse.

In Nepal, there are far too many examples of crimes against women and girls. For instance, Nirmala Panta, 13, was found dead in a sugarcane field — a case which has remained unsolved since 2018. Bhagirathi Bhatta, 17, was choked to death when returning home from school in 2021, and Inisha BK, 16, was found unconscious in the Janagaran Community Forest in Surkhet in early 2026. A similar yet shocking case is that of a 3-year-old Garima, who was found dead inside an abandoned house in Jeetpur in southern Nepal. While these tragic rape and murder cases leave deep scars in Nepal’s national psyche, even more cases go unheard and unreported.

Sparking a nationwide outrage, such cases force the country to confront a collective shame. They raise questions around human morality, diminishing trust and affection in society, and breakdowns in the legal justice system. In the face of these atrocities, women took to the streets, demanding justice and accountability. But their calls fell on deaf ears.
Pratistha Gautam’s story

“I was 11 years old when I was sexually abused by my close maternal uncle for four days,” said Pratishtha Gautam in an online interview with Global Voices in November 2026. Opening up about this incident was a real challenge for her, yet she was committed to sharing her story.

Her childhood was by no means easy. She moved regularly as a child, and at six years old, she was sent to her grandparent’s house for a year because her parents had to move away to address their employment needs. This separation made her feel neglected and she felt that her parents loved her younger brother more. This contributed to a sense of emotional distance and detachment from her family.

Later, at the age of 11, she was left in the care of her mother’s cousin while her younger brother was hospitalized and receiving medical treatment. It was during this time that she experienced sexual abuse at the hands of someone she had known and trusted as a family member, who took away her innocence.

After four days of abuse, she escaped when the abuser fled after she began calling out for help. Finally getting a chance to flee from danger, she “rushed to my room, quickly happened to lock the door by chance, thankfully, and began to scream out to my neighbors.” She had witnessed men mistreating women growing up and feels lucky that her cries weren’t met with indifference.
The abuse only compounded her challenges. As she says, “It was not easy at all.”

The experience has left her with scars: “I have been awakened with nightmares since that incident, making my sleep extremely difficult.” She also suffers from panic attacks when she sees material about sexual abuse. She describes feeling like her heart is swollen and being torn apart. When triggered, she often freezes up and dissociates.

According to research from the American Academy of Pediatrics journal, child sexual abuse can be incredibly detrimental to a person’s long-term mental well-being. Child abuse survivors are more likely to suffer from anxiety disorders, depression, eating disorders and disturbances, sleep disruption and insomnia, and dissociation, as well as adverse physical health conditions and attachment issues, according to the Center of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse.

This highlights the immense scale of pain that many children experience when they are victims of sexual abuse. Not everyone is able to speak out about such abuses. This is particularly true in South Asia, where there is a social stigma around abuse, due to entrenched ideas around “purity.”

She resents suggestions that it is women’s responsibility to not “tempt” men or draw attention to themselves. “Why should we be the ones to cover ourselves up?” she asks. She refuses to hide and stay silent while her abuser “is living free somewhere.” She refuses to remain invisible.

Even as many countries make strides in gender equality, gender-based violence continues to be a major issue. In a 2023 report, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that nearly one in three (31.6 percent) of women worldwide have been subjected to either physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime — roughly 840 million women and girls.

At the root of gender-based violence lies a belief in male superiority. Not all men would openly endorse this belief, yet many see themselves as protectors of the women in their lives: their sisters, mothers, girlfriends, and wives. But this notion of protection is deeply flawed, especially when it comes at the cost of women’s freedom, mobility, access to opportunities, dreams, and agency.

Gautam recognizes this notion in her own upbringing. She had dreams of her own and was ready to chase them, but the universe had a different plan for her. She kept her independence through consistent stubbornness and determination.
A trauma that persists

Today, Gautam lives in Adelaide in South Australia. She suffers from complex PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and works as a mental health clinician helping other survivors of abuse. She reflected, in a heavy tone, on being a thousand miles away from home but safe and independent.
Gautam feeding a child. Image via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.

PTSD and insomnia aren’t the only consequences of her abuse. While she was once married, she struggled to cope with her trauma, and it negatively impacted her relationship, eventually leading to divorce.

As part of her treatment, Gautam has met regularly with psychotherapists over the years. Eventually, even that wasn’t enough. She put everything on hold for a year and gave herself time and space to focus on her mental health. She believes she would have difficulty living a normal life and still struggles with relationships. “I hate men. I used to hate them and still have trust issues,” she said.

Even as she struggles to process her own trauma, she also works to help others recover from abuse and offers pro bono psychological counseling. Being part of the solution has in some ways helped her heal. Her passion as a mental health clinician goes beyond her own individual experiences to the collective — a reminder to be empathetic as humans first.

While she primarily works in Australia, she is also committed to helping women back in her home country of Nepal. She has collaborated with Rakshya Nepal, an organization in Nepal that protects women and girls from sexual exploitation and trafficking.
Reflecting back on the choices she made, she said, “I cannot imagine if I could afford this luxury of mental space if I were not in Australia.”

This is also a testament to how South Asia treats survivors of sexual and physical abuse — even if they gather the courage to speak the truth, too often they are met with judgment and scorn. Part of this is due to limited regard for mental health, but it’s also about entrenched gender roles and strong societal expectations. There is a popular saying in Nepal reflecting these persistent gender dynamics: “timi ta chori manche ho ni” and “chora manche ho ni,” which roughly translates to “you are a girl, and boys will be boys.”
Written by Susmita Aryal
6f2d9f153e249ab8: Following the 2026 state elections, many are predicting that Umno and Perikatan Nasional (PN) will team up and win power in the next general election (GE).

Most analysts see it as an almost certain clash between PH and a PAS-led PN in the peninsula. Some argue that GE16 will be fought primarily on traditional flashpoints: Malay rights, Islamic values, economic delivery, and non-Malay frustrations.
That may be true, but I think this election is more likely to boil down to a dramatic contest of political agility and manoeuvres between Ahmad Zahid Hamidi and Anwar Ibrahim.

While East Malaysia’s blocs in Sabah and Sarawak will—as always—play a decisive kingmaker role post-election to protect local autonomy, the battle to capture Putrajaya itself remains a peninsula-driven contest. Within that crucible, GE16 will essentially be a battle of wills and operational skill between two men who know how to survive at the top.

Zahid's core competency is political engineering. He treats relationships as leverage, public statements as bargaining signals, and possesses a feel for power dynamics that is probably unmatched in modern Malaysian politics.

Yet, while his "blue wave" narrative resonates powerfully with Malay voters, it does not travel cleanly to the urban, mixed, and non-Malay constituencies that ultimately decide a national majority—though Umno relies on its traditional Barisan Nasional coalition mechanisms to manage multi-ethnic seats.

Conversely, Anwar’s strength lies in policy, narrative, and survival. A reformist with international credibility and a coherent platform, Anwar has ridden the waves of triumph and defeat, navigated various crises, and risen to become prime minister.
He is waging a war of attrition, using his control over the national budget and administrative levers to delay the electoral clock while Zahid tries to force an early hand.
To understand why this duel will define GE16, we must look back at how their paths have intertwined over the last three decades.

When the bitter fallout between then-Umno president Mahathir Mohamad and his deputy Anwar erupted in the late 1990s, Zahid—serving as Umno Youth chief—initially backed Anwar. Yet, after Anwar’s sacking in 1998, Zahid quickly pivoted, reconciled with Mahathir, and demonstrated the classic Umno survival instinct: prioritising pragmatism over loyalty.

From that point, Zahid embarked on a meticulously calculated ascent: consolidating his base in Perak, building a formidable personal network, becoming Umno’s deputy president, and finally taking the top spot in 2018.

Following the 2022 humiliation when Umno won just 26 seats, calls for his resignation mounted. He weathered the storm, teamed up with Anwar to secure the post of deputy prime minister, and used his proximity to power to reassert Umno’s relevance.

Anwar, for his part, pursued his long game: forming PKR, driving the Reformasi movement, riding the 2008 opposition surge, and eventually making an uneasy truce with his arch-rival Mahathir to wrest power in 2018. But political betrayals caused Mahathir’s government to collapse, paving the way for short-lived administrations under Muhyiddin Yassin and Ismail Sabri Yaakob.

The inconclusive 2022 general election threw Anwar and Zahid together into an improbable partnership. Zahid secured ministerial perks and shared authority, and by December 2025, the Attorney General’s Chambers granted him a discharge not amounting to an acquittal (DNAA) on the 47 corruption charges involving the Yayasan Akalbudi fund.
Critics blasted the move as a classic manoeuvre to shield allies and buy loyalty, though it has consistently been denied.
Since then, Zahid has supercharged Umno's stature among Malay supporters by leaning into the reliable narrative of Malay unity and perceived threats to Malay dominance.

The resulting PAS-Umno tactical cooperation benefits both parties. This momentum was reflected in the 2026 state elections, though formulas varied: in Johor, BN swept 48 of 56 seats alone (while PN supporters were quietly instructed to back BN in uncontested seats), whereas in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, BN and PN formally shared seats.
True to form, Zahid is keeping all options open by refusing to commit to a formal GE16 pact with PN, executing a masterstroke that forces both PH and PN to compete for Umno's favour.

Simultaneously, he has tightened his internal grip: the Umno Supreme Council has postponed party polls to a date no later than six months after GE16, and an "unconditional open-door" policy has welcomed back former rivals like Khairy Jamaluddin and Hishammuddin Hussein. Zahid is building a broad electoral coalition while keeping his own leadership uncontested.

Demonstrating his pragmatic ambition further, Zahid acknowledged Gabungan Parti Sarawak's (GPS) absolute regional dominance by confirming that BN would sit out the Sarawak state election to respect East Malaysian autonomy and keep the federal focus razor-sharp on the peninsula.

Conversely, Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan has been battling severe internal friction. PKR has suffered heavy blows: high-profile figures like Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad departed to form Parti Bersama Malaysia, Nurul Izzah went on indefinite leave as deputy president, and the party suffered a major rout in Melaka.

Anwar's prospects now hinge heavily on timing. PH’s parliamentary term runs until December 2027, with GE16 legally due by February 2028. Every month of delay buys both sides different advantages: Zahid consolidates his machine, while Anwar attempts to deliver tangible economic relief.
If Anwar can produce visible improvements in the cost of living by late 2027 and push through more reforms, the votes will return.

Furthermore, PH retains a structural edge in the urban and mixed constituencies that decide a national majority. State elections are typically less diverse and more heavily Malay-majority, making the "blue wave" less effective on a national scale.

Moreover, non-Malay support for PH is driven less by uncritical loyalty and more by a structural fear of the alternative (a PAS-led PN). As the Malay vote consolidates behind BN-PN, non-Malay voters increasingly rally behind DAP and PH as a defensive counterweight, keeping PH viable nationally even as it bleeds support in heartland seats.
Also, as seat negotiations between Umno and PAS heat up, deep fractures in the Malay-Muslim vote will be exposed.

Yet, as these electoral calculations play out, Zahid carries a heavy legal overhang. The Court of Appeal allowed the Malaysian Bar's judicial review challenge in May 2026, the Federal Court granted Zahid and the AG leave to appeal in October 2026, and the High Court has slated case management for June 2027, with the full hearing deferred until the Federal Court appeal concludes. It is a sword of Damocles that is certain to become a major campaign issue.

Ultimately, GE16 will be a contest of political operators. The 2026 state elections suggest Zahid holds the momentum. However, Anwar’s control over the electoral timeline, his economic levers, and the structural divide between state and national electorates keep the race wide open.

What began as a clash between reform and patronage has evolved into a masterclass in machine politics versus institutional statecraft. The next general election will not be decided by slogans or promises alone—it will be decided by who plays the sharper game over the next six to twelve months.

52e6204978a8560b: The Najib Razak saga has, in many ways, eclipsed even Anwar Ibrahim’s ‘Reformasi’ struggles, which saw many of us old-timers go through some very harrowing times.
Both were deputy prime ministers and served under Dr Mahathir Mohamad.
Their parallels are striking. Anwar was sacked, charged, convicted and spent time in prison before being pardoned, later rising to become prime minister.
Najib took the opposite route. An Umno prime minister, no less, he lost power, was charged, convicted and served time, before being pardoned twice, albeit conditionally.

Despite the unbridled demonisation of the DAP and non-Malays as traitors out to wreck a nation, it must be stressed that it was a courageous Malay judge—a woman no less—who sent the former Umno president to jail.
Now, there are many “firsts” in this saga.

Najib went on trial in what became known as “the world’s largest kleptocracy case”, a notorious distinction that brought his party and the country the sort of international headlines it could have done without.
Secondly, Najib is the first prime minister to be incarcerated in Malaysia.
And thirdly, this is the first documented house arrest case in the country, even preceding a proposed new law that the government intends to introduce in Parliament.
Now there are many views about the former Pekan MP’s house arrest.
Among them is the perceived double-standard. Why is Najib allowed these perks, while other convicts are not?
There is also the matter of the king’s decision in Najib’s pardon application. Must the king adhere to the pardon board’s advice? And should the minutes have been declassified?
As for the king’s decision to allow Najib to be placed under house arrest, that is his prerogative, one that is enshrined in our Federal Constitution.
He has chosen to exercise it in Najib’s favour for reasons known only to him. Not being privy to that decision, and without any insights into his reasons, it would not be proper to comment on it.
But it has to be emphasised that there is no prefect constitution, no perfect rendition of history, and no perfect interpretation of religion.
Hence, we need to rely on the wisdom and experience of those who make such decisions with the nation’s best interests at heart.
The recent publication of the minutes of that meeting of the pardons board has given the public a rare insight into what transpired and the stance taken by each board member.
That said, the published document should not trigger a blame game.
Whatever one feels about the decision, it must be acknowledged that it went through due process.
If Malaysians believe that process should be improved or changed, the proper avenue is through their elected representatives in the Dewan Rakyat.
For my part, I am satisfied that due process has been observed and therefore respect and accept the decision reached.

Still, I find it comical that Umno has been so worked up over the declassification of the document simply because it was not accompanied by a royal decree, even arguing that the omission was somehow tantamount to disrespecting the Malay rulers.
Has that same respect been shown to Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir amid the seemingly unending constitutional crisis in Negeri Sembilan, a controversy that bears Umno's fingerprints all over it?
The time has come for us to put the brouhaha over Najib's house arrest to rest.
At the end of the day, Najib was convicted for a crime, served some time in jail, applied for a pardon, as allowed by law, and was granted one.
Placing him under house arrest does not erase his criminal conviction.
There is no value in bickering over the merits of the house arrest as it serves no purpose other than to instigate one party and weaponise the issue.
It is time we focused on the more important stuff, like the bread-and-butter issues affecting ordinary Malaysians. That is a far more worthy cause.

9b6b75dea9243402: Tony Pua has apparently discovered a remarkable constitutional innovation: when the king grants clemency against objections, publish the objections and call it accountability. Yet the awkward question remains. Does displaying dissent explain the constitutional decision, or merely provide political cover for those embarrassed by its outcome?
On Nov 18, Pua circulated pages described as declassified minutes from the Sept 18 Federal Territories Pardons Board meeting concerning former prime minister Najib Razak.

According to news reports, Attorney-General Dusuki Mokhtar and federal territories minister Hannah Yeoh opposed house arrest. The king nevertheless approved a conditional pardon. These reported extracts warrant authentication and contextual examination; a Facebook upload is not itself a constitutional certificate.
Let us distinguish three matters politicians seem determined to blend: the right to disagree during deliberations, the authority to decide, and the legality of disclosing deliberations afterwards.

Article 42 establishes the constitutional pardoning framework. Recording objections does not confer a veto. Nor does royal authority automatically exempt officials from explaining how records were classified, accessed and released.

Pua’s intervention invites sharper scrutiny precisely because he presents disclosure as vindication. Vindication of what? That DAP representatives objected? The minutes reportedly establish that much. That the government’s political conscience is therefore spotless? That is a considerably longer leap, requiring evidence rather than screenshots and self-congratulation.

DAP cannot simultaneously celebrate constitutional procedure when it documents ministerial dissent and treat the resulting royal decision as someone else’s political inconvenience. A constitutional monarchy is not a buffet where parties select the minutes they enjoy and leave the decision behind. If dissent was properly recorded, publicly explain it. If the decision was lawful, respect it. Neither proposition requires surrendering criticism of corruption.

Umno is justified in demanding a clear account of the disclosure process. Its leaders have asked whether the documents were officially declassified, who authorised circulation, and whether the palace was consulted. Those are legitimate institutional questions, although assertions that publication necessarily constitutes an insult to the king require a specific legal and factual foundation. Defending royal dignity should strengthen constitutional precision, not replace it with outrage.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim faces the more uncomfortable examination. He has publicly defended every prisoner’s access to the pardon process and acknowledged the king’s constitutional role. Fine words. But was his administration’s handling of disclosure governed by a consistent rule, or by whichever political controversy happened to be burning that week? The public deserves an answer from Putrajaya, not another seminar on principles everyone claims to cherish.

The comparison with Anwar’s 2018 pardon is unavoidable. Wan Saiful Wan Jan has called for those Pardons Board minutes to be released, too. That demand does not prove irregularity in either pardon. It does expose the weakness of selective transparency. If publication serves public confidence today, what principled distinction governs disclosure of earlier proceedings? Privacy, privilege and national security may justify redactions; political convenience is not a constitutional doctrine.

There is an important qualification. Minutes capture deliberation, not necessarily every legal consideration or the full operative instrument. Readers should resist pretending five circulated pages settle all constitutional questions. Officials must establish authenticity, classification status, completeness, and applicable disclosure authority before political protagonists announce their preferred verdict.

My assessment is that this affair tests the government’s credibility more severely than Najib’s political fortunes. A government preaching institutional reform must demonstrate procedures that survive partisan advantage. Publish a reasoned disclosure policy, identify the competent authorising authority, and apply equivalent standards to comparable pardons. Where confidentiality is required, explain its legal basis without exposing protected deliberations.

And Pua? He is entitled to criticise Najib, challenge clemency and defend his former colleagues. He is not entitled to confuse proof of opposition with proof of governmental consistency. The former may fit neatly into a social media post; the latter demands accountability across administrations, personalities, and inconvenient precedents.
The king does not require politicians to manufacture unanimity. The Constitution requires institutions to understand their responsibilities.
Umno should defend that distinction firmly; DAP and PH should answer it without theatrical evasion; Anwar should insist upon rules rather than improvisation.
When constitutional records become partisan ammunition, the real scandal is not disagreement. It is a government unable to explain who loaded the weapon, under what authority, and why only now.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

8f13969a68ed3f91: Having agreed to new peace talks with Ukrainian and American representatives earlier this month, Russian negotiators suddenly wanted to discuss the European security order, too.
It was an obvious attempt to divert attention from the urgent need, after almost five years, for a ceasefire in Russian president Vladimir Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine.
While the inept US negotiating duo of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff seemed to go along with the Russian proposal, the Europeans saw right through it.
They pointed out that there is already an agreed European security order, to which Russia is a signatory. The only problem is that Russia is blatantly violating it. That is what must be discussed.

The European security order is basically no different from what the United Nations Charter established in 1945. Coming after two bitter, brutal world wars, the UN Charter codified the territorial integrity of all states, and identified the crime of aggression as the ultimate violation of international law.

But the European order that gradually emerged towards the end of the Cold War went further than this. Through the laborious negotiations leading up to the Helsinki Accords in 1975, and through the process that produced the Paris Charter of 1990, Europeans added provisions on democracy, human rights, and economic cooperation to the basic security architecture.

Of course, there were occasional disagreements about how to implement these agreements’ requirements, and in both Georgia and Moldova in the 2000s, Russia openly violated provisions barring the presence of a country’s armed forces on the territory of another without its consent.

These moves sparked bitter debates, with Russia eventually calling for revisions to the European security order. The Kremlin, for obvious reasons, objected to the provisions concerning human rights and elections, and demanded that they be deleted or substantially diluted.

It wasn’t difficult to see why. A series of “colour revolutions” had started to sweep through the region, most notably in Georgia and Ukraine, where protesters demanded democratic reforms, the rule of law, and closer links with democratic Europe.
Upon returning to the presidency after a brief stint as prime minister to circumvent constitutional limits, Putin himself was confronted with huge demonstrations in Moscow.

With a democratic wave sweeping much of the world at the time, the Kremlin understood that the colour revolutions in other countries had inspired pro-democracy demonstrations on its own streets. More to the point, it knew that pro-democratic forces could count on moral support from the West.

Russia tried to force new negotiations to suppress previously agreed commitments on democracy, but no one else would support such an effort. The order that had been established at the summits in Helsinki and Paris stood firm.

More recently, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has called attention to a provision from a 1999 Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe document, which holds that signatories “will not strengthen their security at the expense of the security of other states”.

Yet he completely ignores another provision from the same document, which reaffirms “the inherent right of each and every participating state to be free to choose or change its security arrangements, including treaties of alliance”.
Such cynical cherry picking is dishonest even by Lavrov’s standards. Membership in Nato or the European Union clearly preserves peace and in no way threatens Russia.

Democratisation in other countries may well inspire those seeking democratic change inside Russia, but that is not the democratising countries’ fault or problem, nor does it endanger Russia’s security.
Putin is now left trying to roll back various European countries’ security choices, and thus their sovereignty. This is obviously a non-starter.

Finland and Sweden chose to enter Nato not to attack Russia, but because Russia had just launched a full-scale invasion of another European neighbour. No sane person is under any illusion about cause and effect.

One hopes that at some point there will be an opening to return to confidence-building and arms-control measures. But with Russian guns blazing and Russian bombs falling over another European country’s civilian centres, now is obviously not the time.

The European security order’s foundational principle is to reject aggression and respect other countries’ territorial integrity. There is no need to revise that order, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to accept it.
In the next round of talks, European representatives will demand an immediate end to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Until that happens, there is nothing else to talk about.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.

dc93da4cf6a361d8: Over 223,700 children have dropped out of school in Cameroon’s Northwest and Southwest regions, while 2,463 schools are non-operational
Originally published on Global Voices
A general view of Buea's OIC Market in the Southwest Region of Cameroon, where displaced families sell goods to support their livelihoods. Photo by Cynthia Ebot Takang. Used with permission.

For children displaced by Cameroon’s ongoing armed Anglophone conflict, reaching safety has not ended the struggle. In Buea, the capital of Cameroon’s Southwest region, some children are balancing school with market trading to help their families survive.

“At least here in Buea, there are no gunshots, and we do not have to hide in the bush,” says 11-year-old Lorane in an interview with Global Voices, describing the relative safety his family found after fleeing their home in Cameroon’s conflict-affected Southwest Region.

The move brought the children to a calmer environment where they could resume schooling and live with less fear of armed violence. But leaving their communities also meant losing homes, familiar surroundings, friendships and, for some, years of education. In Buea, the struggle to rebuild family livelihoods has introduced another responsibility to their lives: helping their parents earn a living.
A safer place, but a childhood reshaped by displacement

The Anglophone crisis in Cameroon began in 2016, when teachers and lawyers began protesting over the perceived marginalization of English-language education and common-law systems, which they say favored French. This escalated into wider demonstrations and a government crackdown. In 2017, the situation deteriorated into armed conflict between government forces and separatist groups seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions as a state commonly referred to as Ambazonia. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that between 2.1 and 2.2 million people have been displaced due to the violence and insecurity.

At Buea’s OIC Market, children from displaced families sell bleach, puff-puff, plantains, ginger, garlic, and oranges, particularly during weekends and before school. Some travel from neighboring communities to help their parents sell goods, while others work around family-owned stalls.

For 14-year-old Joy, this means traveling from Mutengene to Buea on weekends to sell sachets of bleach. Her mother buys the bleach in bulk and repackages it into smaller sachets, which Joy sells for CFA 100 (about USD 0.17) each. She says daily sales can reach CFA 10,000–15,000 (about USD 16.81–25.21), helping support the household and her siblings.

Joy has been working since her family fled their village when she was in Class Five. “They were shooting guns in my village, so my mum had to bring us here so we could continue school,” she says. She has since become used to the routine, which allows her to contribute to the family while continuing her education.

For 14-year-old Sidoine, displacement meant losing four years of schooling. Her family fled Ekona after their house was burned while they were away at the farm. She remembers hiding in the bushes when they heard attacks were coming, unsure what would happen next. Her family eventually left their hometown, Ekona, for Buea, joining thousands of others who have had to rebuild their lives away from their roots. A well-wisher eventually helped her enroll in school in Buea.
Although the family sometimes visits their farm to collect food, it has not been possible to return permanently. Sidoine misses her former home and friends.
Rebuilding a family livelihood

For younger children, displacement has also changed family routines. Twelve-year-old Michelle sells plantains while waiting for his mother to return from church. His 11-year-old cousin, Lorane, sometimes accompanies him. The two help their parents attract customers, particularly on weekends.
They also miss people they left behind in Ekona, including their grandmother, who died during a raid as a result of the crisis.

Susan Achuagoh, a mother of five whose house was burned during the conflict, has had to rebuild her livelihood as an orange seller in Buea. She gives her children small quantities of oranges to sell while she remains at her stall. This helps supplement their family income.
“I sell oranges; I give them small things to walk around with while I stay at the stall,” she shared in an interview with Global Voices. “If they do not help like that, it will not go at all.”

Her children’s education was interrupted for more than three years during the conflict. Another mother, Mami Blessing, says her children’s schooling was also disrupted and that they now help her at the market as the family struggles to make ends meet.
The cost of conflict

Godiva Ndang epse Limene, Education and Partnerships Officer at Street Child UK-Cameroon, says the prolonged crisis in the Northwest and Southwest has increasingly become a crisis of childhood, affecting education, protection, and development.

Children exposed to armed violence, displacement, and repeated insecurity may experience anxiety, difficulty concentrating, and social withdrawal. Taking on economic responsibilities can add to these pressures. Ndang says work that takes up time needed for learning, rest, and play can affect children’s cognitive, emotional, social, and physical development.

She stresses that helping in a family business is not automatically child labor. The distinction depends on the child’s age, the nature and duration of the activity, the risks involved, and whether it interferes with education, health, rest, or development.

The right to education is only one of the rights affected. Children also have a right to rest, leisure, and play, as well as protection from economic exploitation. For those uprooted from their communities, maintaining friendships, participating in cultural life, and developing a sense of belonging are also important parts of growing up.
Learning spaces offer a route back to education

The scale of the disruption remains significant. Figures from the Regional Delegations of Basic Education cited by UNICEF in September 2026 show that 223,749 children were completely out of school in the Northwest and Southwest, while 2,463 schools were non-operational. Of these, 2,005 were in the Northwest and 458 in the Southwest.

To educate children in conflict-affected communities, local partners including TeenAlive, the Foundation for Inclusive Education (FIED), Strategic Humanitarian Services (SHUMAS), and the Authentique Memorial Empowerment Foundation (AMEF) support Mobile Neighborhood Learning Corners and Satellite Learning Corners. These are established in accessible locations such as village chiefs’ homes, churches, schools, and community verandas.

The program has supported close to 100 learning corners across the two regions. Other education interventions include help with school enrollment, uniforms, and learning materials, as well as Teaching at the Right Level, a tutoring program.

Street Child also combines education with other forms of support. Its girls’ resilience and empowerment work provides displaced adolescent girls with life skills, literacy, and vocational training, alongside start-up kits and mental health assistance. Its Play for Peace initiative, supported by the FIFA Foundation, uses sports to promote peace, health, and education in conflict-affected communities.

Ndang says children also need psychosocial support, safe learning environments, and opportunities to play and interact with their peers. She adds that helping caregivers rebuild their livelihoods matters because reducing economic pressure on families can lessen the burden on children.
Ambition despite displacement
Despite interruptions to their education and the responsibilities they have taken on, the children interviewed for this story continue to speak about their goals and ambitions.

Eliot, 14, who helps his mother sell oranges on weekends, wants to become an engineer. Sidoine hopes to study law, although she worries about the years she lost in school. Vickians, 12, who fled Lebialem and now studies computer science, wants to become a computer engineer.
On weekends, Vickians sells miondo, a cassava-based delicacy, with her parents. Her family continues to make sacrifices to keep her in school, and she remains determined to pursue her education.

At the start of the 2026–2027 academic year, Southwest Governor Bernard Okalia Bilai said the authorities wanted children across the region to have equal access to education and learning facilities, despite differences in school attendance between urban and rural communities. His remarks, reported in this September 2026 interview on the reopening of schools, underline the challenge facing the region: ensuring that displacement and insecurity do not determine whether children can access education.

Reporting note: The names used for the children in this story are pseudonyms to protect their identities. No photographs of the children have been published. Consent was obtained from parents before the interviews were conducted.
Written by Cynthia Ebot Takang

ce467387ca06079a: From Jonathan Edward
The narrative surrounding Chinese industrial overcapacity is being used as a convenient scapegoat for domestic economic stagnation.

The recent comment by Mazli Noor, China’s overcapacity, a test of Malaysia’s resilience, exemplifies this point by suggesting that Malaysia must erect trade barriers, tighten anti-dumping regimes, and mandate local content rules to shield domestic producers from Chinese imports misses the fundamental mechanics of global trade.
If Malaysia wishes to thrive, it must either compete on the same terms through aggressive state-backed industrial policy or pivot towards producing different, higher-value goods and services.
Attempting to insulate uncompetitive industries behind regulatory walls is not a strategy for resilience, but a guarantee for economic obsolescence.
'Overcapacity' is a politically loaded talking point
The very term "overcapacity" is a politically loaded construct designed to frame superior manufacturing efficiency as a market distortion.

In April 2024, former US Treasury secretary Janet Yellen warned that Chinese industrial overcapacity threatened global markets and Western workers - a claim China rejected, crediting its export success to market forces, scale, and supply chain integration rather than unfair manipulation.

State support has undeniably played a major role in China's industrial ascent, yet there is nothing stopping Malaysia from adopting similar measures if it genuinely wishes to dominate heavy industries like crude steel.
If replicating China’s state-capitalist model is neither fiscally practical nor politically desirable for Putrajaya, then market forces must be allowed to dictate the outcome.
The failure of domestic protectionism

Malaysia already knows the consequences of coddling legacy industries. For decades, protectionist policies and selective state support have benefitted a handful of well-connected conglomerates without translating into broader economic dynamism.
Instead, these sheltered entities have repeatedly devolved into sluggish, uncompetitive monopolies that pass higher costs onto Malaysian consumers and downstream businesses.

It is an uncontroversial local reality that shielding domestic firms from foreign competition removes the very pressure required to innovate. Calling for anti-dumping duties and stricter customs hurdles will merely entrench inefficiency while penalising every Malaysian household and manufacturer that relies on affordable inputs.
Moving up the manufacturing value chain

Trying to compete head-to-head with the world’s largest manufacturing powerhouse on basic commodities like crude steel or bulk plastics is economic suicide. Rather than lamenting low capacity utilisation in legacy blast furnaces, Malaysia must upskill and upgrade its industrial base.

Modern manufacturing technologies, such as precision computer numerical control (CNC) machining, industrial 3D printing, and advanced metallurgy, allow smaller, agile firms to produce specialised components and bespoke widgets made from exotic materials.

Instead of churning out raw base stock, Malaysian manufacturers should be supplying precision-engineered parts for global aerospace, medical devices, and specialised equipment for the regional oil and gas sector.
Unlocking agriculture, aquaculture, and services

Malaysia’s economic future does not depend on matching China factory for factory when vast domestic sectors remain chronically underutilised. Consider agriculture and aquaculture, both of which possess immense export potential. For years, prime agricultural land has been squandered on speculative property developments that sit unsold, or cleared under questionable pretexts for logging.

Meanwhile, our rivers suffer from heavy sedimentation caused by upstream deforestation, alongside rampant chemical pollution and garbage dumping. Properly managed, Malaysia’s waterways could anchor a lucrative freshwater aquaculture export industry.

Malaysians are an inventive and entrepreneurial people. We have even successfully bred sturgeon in tropical conditions to produce luxury caviar. Imagine what could be achieved if environmental stewardship and agricultural land reform were treated as national priorities.

Similarly, Malaysia holds substantial natural advantages in high-value services. With a multilingual workforce and established legal and financial frameworks, the nation is well-positioned to expand aggressively into regional tech support, fintech, cross-border legal services, and financial advisory. Competing in brainpower and service delivery bypasses the physical scale advantages of Chinese manufacturing entirely.
Geopolitical hypocrisy and trade realities

Singling out China for its industrial might also ignores the broader geopolitical reality facing Southeast Asia. The US has swung towards unpredictable unilateralism, weaponising tariffs and imposing sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence chips and advanced technologies. Its actions in the Middle East have kicked off the energy crisis the whole world is reeling from.

At the same time, the European Union is grappling with severe deindustrialisation and has become an increasingly cumbersome trade partner, imposing stringent regulatory barriers that directly threaten Malaysia’s environmental sovereignty and palm oil exports.

Why, then, should Malaysia lecture China for being a cost-effective manufacturer and a vital trading partner when we do not publicly chastise the US for its tech blockades or the European Union for its protectionist green mandates? Criticising the one major power that still possesses the capacity to produce at scale and low cost while offering a massive consumer market for Malaysian exports defies basic economic logic.
Adaptability over obstruction

Complaining about how well-resourced the competition happens to be reflects a defeatist mindset. True progress comes from pulling oneself up, not attempting to drag a competitor down. If Malaysia wants to empower local industry, it should immediately deregulate sectors where bureaucratic red tape suffocates enterprise, slash corporate and manufacturing taxes, and provide agile firms with the land, energy, and capital needed to scale.
Trying to restrain China’s industrial output is an exercise in futility, and attempting to freeze market dynamics is like trying to stop time itself.

Global manufacturing is constantly in motion. When a dominant power shifts its focus towards new frontiers, nimble competitors step in to fill the vacated space. Malaysian manufacturers must embrace this reality, pivot away from lost battles in heavy commodities, and capture the specialised, high-value niches where they can genuinely win.
Jonathan Edward is a media practitioner and an FMT reader.

4d98effdc3566e59: The dominant Nepali food narrative overlooks the diverse regional histories and culinary traditions of Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Timu khole, wild mushroom soup. Photo by Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat, a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”
The Foundation, established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha, a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook, authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh, the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.
Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end. As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people, and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya, a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.
SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?
When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.
The author in conversation with women's group members. Photo via Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country, and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.
The cover of The Lekhali Cookbook. Photo by Sanjib Chaudhary. Used with permission.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

For many Indigenous communities, the problem has also been due to others writing about their history. Of course, there are some very rare scholars who have done a fine job, but in the case of our own history, there is now an immense effort to establish or re-establish our origin account. It’s very saddening to have to read about some of these accounts. And then there is also the process of verifying and fact-checking, and that takes a lot of time.

The Lekhali Cookbook came into being due to a generous grant from the British Council. A lot of the work had been conducted prior to receiving the grant, but it allowed us to visit the villages in the central Himalayas and work with aama samuha [translated as “mothers’ groups,” acting as local women’s collectives] who are heavily involved in the food production process. Based on the consultation with the groups, we collected the recipes of the eight villages of Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, and Gorkha.

In the book, we have some unique recipes that many people do not know, such as the foraged panyu (wild rhubarb), kru (yak sausage), yak curry with satu, or farsi ko bhat eaten with sattu up in the high Gorkha hills.
SC: What do you think the future of Indigenous food will look like in a decade's time? What should Indigenous communities, in your opinion, do to preserve and promote their food heritage?

BG: I think we have immense challenges ahead of us. Every year, these challenges seem to be only growing more and more. We only have to look at the recent disasters; it’s quite terrifying for the people who are living in these landscapes.

For several reasons, it’s crucial that we recognize that our situation is changing and that it is very fragile, and we have to be alert to this changing situation. So much has already changed, and within this framework we have to think of how we are going to adapt to our new circumstances, whether it is living in the city, establishing a relationship with urban life, learning to operate in a language that is not your mother tongue, learning technology, issues of sustainability, and so on.

In the midst of this vast change from our previous ancestral way of life, how are we going to hold ourselves as people with a distinct way of living, language, and culture? Moreover, how are we going to maintain the values that have been passed down to us from our ancestors? How willing are we to work for our collective welfare to protect our cultural and food heritage in this sea of change? Because without addressing these questions or without internalizing them, we cannot have real progress.
Written by Sanjib Chaudhary

b59750cc64703019: Muhammad Fajri/GettyAfter a year of record-breaking weather and a “super” El Niño underway, there’s no doubt climate extremes are wreaking havoc across the globe. For decades, scientists have warned us this would happen. Their research made the case for reducing fossil fuel dependence. And we’ve relied on their expertise to assess the severity and extent of climate change. But a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries is now obstructing the publication of a key scientific report from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). This threatens global cooperation on tackling the climate crisis. And it has created deep concern at the COP31 climate summit, currently in its final hours in Turkey, also known as Türkiye. A truly global report First, it helps to understand why this report is so significant. The IPCC is the UN body for assessing the science related to climate change. Established in 1988, it provides political leaders with independent scientific assessments on climate change and strategies for response. This panel has produced six pivotal reports to date, which have collated and reviewed the latest knowledge on climate change science. And over the past two years, more than 640 experts from around the world have been meeting to write the seventh. The authors are leading researchers who volunteer their time. More than half of the authors working on the current seventh report, called the Seventh Assessment Report, or AR7, are from developing countries. I am a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports in the working group that looks at impacts, vulnerability and adaptation. Work on this seventh report kicked off in December 2024, and its timeline for completion was never officially finalised. What’s the hold-up? Originally, the plan was for the seventh report to be released in 2028. But five countries are objecting to this timeline and pushing for a later release in 2029. India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Kenya and China are ostensibly arguing that countries from the global south lack the resources and capacity to meet the current deadline. However, these countries also happen to be among the world’s largest fossil fuel producers. If recent reports are anything to go by, the evidence of global warming in this seventh report is likely to be alarming. It will highlight the evidence for much greater action, including deep and urgent reduction in fossil fuel production and use. Extending the release date means IPCC contributors would have even more information they would have to assess. This delay would increase, not alleviate, the demands of authorship and reviewing for those contributors from developing nations. The disagreement resulted in the suspension of the latest IPCC meeting in October in Ethiopia, with no confirmed timeline for the report release or budget for 2027. This threatens the very existence of the IPCC. Nations seeking delay argue that tight timelines are unfair to developing countries. But the least developed countries (LDC), a group comprised of 44 nations, expressed “deep disappointment” when the meeting in Ethiopia was suspended. Why the deadline matters Every five years, the UN’s climate body does a global stocktake of how effectively the world is responding to climate change. Intended to ramp up climate action, these stocktakes take a long hard look at the state of the planet, identify the gaps in our approach and suggest a path forward. To be truly effective, these must be based on the latest science. Delaying the seventh report would mean the most recent science is not fed into the 2028 global stocktake. This has grave implications for future climate action, and any delay in our response could have catastrophic effects on the wellbeing of planetary and human health. Science vs politics While major fossil-fuel-emitting countries often attempt to impede phaseout efforts, undermining the IPCC follows a recent trend of discrediting science for political ends. After a UN report in September found that limiting global warming to 1.5°C was no longer possible, Saudi Arabia jumped to question the credibility of the science, contending the research was not peer-reviewed. In fact, the report had been written over the course of a year by 44 experts, and reviewed by a further 44. Conflict at COP31 Despite opposition to delaying the IPCC report, those pushing for it have remained unmoved at COP31. Speaking to media at the summit, former US Vice President Al Gore accused Saudi Arabia of trying to sabotage the IPCC’s work. “Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the IPCC in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” he said. At climate negotiations where the phrase “fossil fuels” is routinely vetoed from the text, finding a resolution to the IPCC issue has even broader implications. If countries can’t agree on this, how will nearly 200 countries agree on a robust final COP31 outcome? Seeking resolution While the clock ticks down on the COP31 negotiations, a resolution to the IPCC issue is unlikely in Turkey. However, it is hoped a timeline and budget can be nailed down at meetings in early December. As the world’s most authoritative global body on climate change, the role the IPCC plays in driving climate action is critical to our future wellbeing. And the science in this seventh report will be fundamental to a truly effective global stocktake. In a time when the world often feels divided, settling this issue amicably and in good faith would offer countries a much-needed reminder that we are capable of cooperation in pursuit of a better future.
